A.3.2 Proofs of Cors. 4.3 and 4.4

Proof of the Mahalanobis energy score propriety

As the Mahalanobis distance ∥⋅∥Σ−1\|\cdot\|_{\Sigma^{-1}} appears in both corollaries, we wish to show that the β\beta-th power of the Mahalanobis distance

dΣ−1​(zi,zj)=‖zi−zj‖Σ−1=(zi−zj)⊤​Σ−1​(zi−zj)d_{\Sigma^{-1}}(z_{i},z_{j})=\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}=\sqrt{(z_{i}-z_{j})^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(z_{i}-z_{j})}

is a conditionally negative definite (CND) kernel, as well as develop some general machinery. We assume Σ\Sigma to be a symmetric positive definite (PD) matrix Σ≻0\Sigma\succ 0, so Σ−1\Sigma^{-1} exists and is symmetric PD.

A real-valued function gg on ℝd×ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d} is said to be a conditionally negative definite (CND) kernel if it is (i) symmetric in its arguments and (ii)

∑i=1n∑j=1nai​aj​g​(zi,zj)≤0\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{i}a_{j}g\left(z_{i},z_{j}\right)\leq 0

for all positive integers nn, all z1,…,znz_{1},\ldots,z_{n}, and all a1,…,an∈ℝa_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\in\mathbb{R} that sum to 00 (this is the “conditionally” part).

To show symmetry, we can simply write:

g⁡(zj,zi)\displaystyle g(z_{j},z_{i}) =∥zj−zi∥Σ−1β=(⟨Σ−1/2(zj−zi),Σ−1/2(zj−zi)⟩)β2\displaystyle=\|z_{j}-z_{i}\|^{\beta}_{\Sigma^{-1}}=\left(\langle\Sigma^{-1/2}(z_{j}-z_{i}),\Sigma^{-1/2}(z_{j}-z_{i})\rangle\right)^{\tfrac{\beta}{2}}
=(⟨Σ−1/2zj,Σ−1/2zj⟩−2⟨Σ−1/2zj,Σ−1/2zi⟩+⟨Σ−1/2zi,Σ−1/2zi⟩)β2\displaystyle=\left(\langle\Sigma^{-1/2}z_{j},\Sigma^{-1/2}z_{j}\rangle-2\langle\Sigma^{-1/2}z_{j},\Sigma^{-1/2}z_{i}\rangle+\langle\Sigma^{-1/2}z_{i},\Sigma^{-1/2}z_{i}\rangle\right)^{\tfrac{\beta}{2}}
=‖zi−zj‖Σ−1β=g⁡(zi,zj)\displaystyle=\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|^{\beta}_{\Sigma^{-1}}=g(z_{i},z_{j})
β=2\beta=2 case:

For the second requirement, let’s begin with the β=2\beta=2 case:

∑i=1n∑j=1naiajg(zj,zi)=∑i=1nai∑j=1naj(∥Σ−1/2zi∥2−2⟨Σ−1/2zj,Σ−1/2zi⟩+∥Σ−1/2zj∥2)=\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{i}a_{j}~g(z_{j},z_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{j}\big(\|\Sigma^{-1/2}z_{i}\|^{2}-2\langle\Sigma^{-1/2}z_{j},\Sigma^{-1/2}z_{i}\rangle+\|\Sigma^{-1/2}z_{j}\|^{2}\big)=
∑i=1nai∑j=1naj(∥Σ−1/2zi∥2+∥Σ−1/2zj∥2)⏟A−2​∑i=1nai​∑j=1naj​zj⊤​Σ−1​zi⏟B≤?0\displaystyle\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{j}\big(\|\Sigma^{-1/2}z_{i}\|^{2}+\|\Sigma^{-1/2}z_{j}\|^{2}\big)}_{A}-\underbrace{2\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{j}z_{j}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}z_{i}}_{B}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{\leq}}0

For the terms in A, we notice that:

∑i,jai​aj​zi⊤​Σ−1​zi=∑iai​zi⊤​Σ−1​zi​∑jaj⏟= 0=0,\sum_{i,j}a_{i}a_{j}\,z_{i}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}z_{i}=\sum_{i}a_{i}\,z_{i}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}z_{i}\;\underbrace{\sum_{j}a_{j}}_{=\,0}=0,

and vice-versa for the zjz_{j} norm term.

Thus, we are left with the term in B:

−2∑i=1nai∑j=1naj⟨Σ−1/2zj,Σ−1/2zi⟩=−2(∑i=1naizi)⊤Σ−1(∑j=1najzj)≤0,\displaystyle-2\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{j}\langle\Sigma^{-1/2}z_{j},\Sigma^{-1/2}z_{i}\rangle=-2(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}z_{i})^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{j}z_{j})\leq 0,

Since Σ−1\Sigma^{-1} is PD, the above quadratic form is nonnegative and the expression is ≤0\leq 0 after multiplication by -2. Together with Theorem 4 in Gneiting and Raftery [12], this gives propriety of the scoring rule (Eq. 9) at β=2\beta=2.

∎

General case — β∈(0,2)\beta\in(0,2):

First of all, we note that the Mahalanobis norm is not a CND kernel for β>2\beta>2:

Let (a1,a2,a3)=(1,1,−2)(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3})=(1,1,-2) and z1=zz_{1}=z, z2=wz_{2}=w, z3=z¯=Δz+w2z_{3}=\bar{z}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Delta}}{{=}}\tfrac{z+w}{2}, so ∑iai=0\sum_{i}a_{i}=0. Since z¯\bar{z} is the midpoint of zz and ww, the three nonzero pairwise distances are

‖z1−z2‖Σ−1=‖z−w‖Σ−1,‖z1−z3‖Σ−1=‖z2−z3‖Σ−1=12​‖z−w‖Σ−1.\|z_{1}-z_{2}\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}=\|z-w\|_{\Sigma^{-1}},\qquad\|z_{1}-z_{3}\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}=\|z_{2}-z_{3}\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\|z-w\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}.

The diagonal terms vanish, and by symmetry each (i,j)(i,j) term can be paired with the corresponding (j,i)(j,i) term. Therefore,

∑i=13∑j=13ai​aj​‖zi−zj‖Σ−1β\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{3}\sum_{j=1}^{3}a_{i}a_{j}\,\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{\beta} =2​[a1​a2​‖z1−z2‖Σ−1β+a1​a3​‖z1−z3‖Σ−1β+a2​a3​‖z2−z3‖Σ−1β]\displaystyle=2\left[a_{1}a_{2}\|z_{1}-z_{2}\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{\beta}+a_{1}a_{3}\|z_{1}-z_{3}\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{\beta}+a_{2}a_{3}\|z_{2}-z_{3}\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{\beta}\right]
=2​[‖z−w‖Σ−1β−2​(12​‖z−w‖Σ−1)β−2​(12​‖z−w‖Σ−1)β]\displaystyle=2\left[\|z-w\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{\beta}-2\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\|z-w\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}\right)^{\beta}-2\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\|z-w\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}\right)^{\beta}\right]
=2​‖z−w‖Σ−1β​(1−22−β).\displaystyle=2\|z-w\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{\beta}\left(1-2^{2-\beta}\right).

The CND inequality would require 1−22−β≤01-2^{2-\beta}\leq 0, equivalently β≤2\beta\leq 2. Thus, for β>2\beta>2, the sum is strictly positive whenever z≠wz\neq w, which violates the CND inequality for every Σ≻0\Sigma\succ 0.

∎

Now, we tackle the general case for β∈(0,2)\beta\in(0,2): For this, we reproduce a classical result due to Schoenberg [31], using a more modern reference found in Berg [2].

We will be using the concept of a Bernstein function, which is a 𝒞∞{\mathcal{C}}^{\infty} function whose derivative is completely monotone. Such functions φ\varphi admit the Levy-Khinchin representation (Def. 5.1 in [2]):

φ⁡(t)=a+b​t+∫0∞(1−e−t​s)​μ​(𝑑s),\varphi(t)\;=\;a+b\,t+\int_{0}^{\infty}\big(1-e^{-ts}\big)\,\mu(ds),

for some a,b≥0a,b\geq 0 and a positive measure μ\mu on (0,∞)(0,\infty).

Further, note that φ⁡(t)=tα\varphi(t)=t^{\alpha} is Bernstein ∀α∈(0,1]\forall\alpha\in(0,1] (Example on p. 16 in [2]).

Next, we claim that the composition of a Bernstein function and a CND kernel is a CND kernel.

To see this, use the Levy-Khinchin representation. Denote for the CND kernel g⁡(zi,zj)=Δgi​jg(z_{i},z_{j})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Delta}}{{=}}g_{ij}. By the Levy-Khinchin representation:

∑i,jai​aj​φ∘gi​j=∑i,jai​aj​φ​(gi​j)=a​∑i,jai​aj+b​∑i,jai​aj​gi​j+∫0∞∑i,jai​aj​(1−e−s​gi​j)​μ​(𝑑s).\sum_{i,j}a_{i}a_{j}~\varphi\circ g_{ij}=\sum_{i,j}a_{i}a_{j}\,\varphi\big(g_{ij}\big)=a\sum_{i,j}a_{i}a_{j}+b\sum_{i,j}a_{i}a_{j}\,g_{ij}+\int_{0}^{\infty}\sum_{i,j}a_{i}a_{j}\big(1-e^{-sg_{ij}}\big)\,\mu(ds). (38)

Next, we use Schoenberg’s theorem (Thm. 2.2 in [2]):

A function gg is CND ⇔\Leftrightarrow exp⁡(−s​g)\exp(-sg) is positive definite for all s>0s>0.

So, denoting e−s​gi​je^{-sg_{ij}} as the PD kernel Ks​(zi,zj)K_{s}(z_{i},z_{j}), we have for the terms in Eq. 38:

  • •

    a​∑i,jai​aj=a​∑iai⏟=0​∑jaj⏟=0≤0a\sum_{i,j}a_{i}a_{j}=a\underbrace{\sum_{i}a_{i}}_{=0}\underbrace{\sum_{j}a_{j}}_{=0}\leq 0

  • •

    b​∑i,jai​aj​gi​j≤0b\sum_{i,j}a_{i}a_{j}g_{ij}\leq 0 since b≥0b\geq 0 and gg is CND.

  • •

    ∑i,jai​aj​(1−Ks​(zi,zj))=(∑iai)2⏟= 0−∑i,jai​aj​Ks​(zi,zj)≤ 0.\sum_{i,j}a_{i}a_{j}\big(1-K_{s}(z_{i},z_{j})\big)=\underbrace{\Big(\sum_{i}a_{i}\Big)^{2}}_{=\,0}\;-\;\sum_{i,j}a_{i}a_{j}K_{s}(z_{i},z_{j})\;\leq\;0.

Integration of the nonpositive term above (∀s\forall s) with respect to the positive measure μ\mu is thus nonpositive. We thus have that a composition of a Bernstein function and a CND kernel is a CND kernel.

∎

We will first use this to prove that the Mahalanobis norm is a CND kernel for β∈(0,2)\beta\in(0,2), and thus the corresponding energy score is a proper scoring rule.

Let α=β/2∈(0,1)\alpha=\beta/2\in(0,1), and denote kβ=(k2)αk_{\beta}=(k_{2})^{\alpha}, and

k2​(z,w)=‖L​z−L​w‖22=‖z−w‖Σ−12,k_{2}(z,w)\;=\;\|Lz-Lw\|_{2}^{2}=\|z-w\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2},

where we are using the Cholesky decomposition Σ−1=L⊤​L\Sigma^{-1}=L^{\top}L.

Using Schoenberg’s theorem (see above) again, k2k_{2} is CND as the corresponding factor e−s​‖u−u′‖22e^{-s\|u-u^{\prime}\|_{2}^{2}} is the well-known PD Gaussian kernel for u=L​zu=Lz and u′=L​wu^{\prime}=Lw.

Thus we have ‖z−w‖Σ−1β=kβ=tα∘k2\|z-w\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{\beta}=k_{\beta}=t^{\alpha}\circ k_{2} is CND by the composition rule for β∈(0,2)\beta\in(0,2). Then, following Theorem 4 in Gneiting and Raftery [12], the corresponding scoring rule (Eq. 9) is proper.

∎

For strict propriety, we reference Theorem 5 in Gneiting and Raftery [12]. It requires the scoring rule to be expressible as:

S⁡(P,w)=𝔼Z∼P​[ψ⁡(‖Z−w‖22)]−12​𝔼Z,Z′​∼iid​P​[ψ⁡(‖Z−Z′‖22)]S(P,w)={\mathbb{E}}_{Z\sim P}[\psi\left(\|Z-w\|_{2}^{2}\right)]-\tfrac{1}{2}{\mathbb{E}}_{Z,Z^{\prime}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P}[\psi\left(\|Z-Z^{\prime}\|_{2}^{2}\right)]

for some ψ\psi continuous on [0,∞)[0,\infty) and ψ′\psi^{\prime} completely monotone and not constant.

We have, for T⁡(z)=L​zT(z)=Lz:

‖z−w‖Σ−1β=‖T⁡(z)−T⁡(w)‖2β=ψ⁡(‖T⁡(z)−T⁡(w)‖22),ψ⁡(t)=tβ/2\|z-w\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{\beta}=\|T(z)-T(w)\|_{2}^{\beta}=\psi\left(\|T(z)-T(w)\|_{2}^{2}\right),\quad\psi(t)=t^{\beta/2}

ψ⁡(t)=tβ/2\psi(t)=t^{\beta/2} is the example given for Theorem 5 in Gneiting and Raftery [12]. Since T⁡(z)=L​zT(z)=Lz is invertible, equality of the whitened distributions is equivalent to equality of the original ones, so strictness transfers to the originals. Hence, the Mahalanobis energy score is, much like the ordinary energy score, strictly proper for β∈(0,2)\beta\in(0,2).

∎

β=2\beta=2 case for the generalized Gaussian

We show the collapse of the generalized energy distance DρD_{\rho} as stated in Cor. 4.3. At β=2\beta=2 the induced discrepancy is ρ⁡(z,w)=‖z−w‖Σ−12\rho(z,w)=\|z-w\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}; PP, QQ have finite second moments throughout (the finite ρ\rho-moment class at β=2\beta=2).

We use two standard facts. A positive definite reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) kernel kk is said to generate the discrepancy ρ\rho if

ρ⁡(z,w)=k⁡(z,z)+k⁡(w,w)−2​k​(z,w).\rho(z,w)=k(z,z)+k(w,w)-2\,k(z,w).

First, Theorem 22 in Sejdinovic et al. [32] states that for any generating RKHS kernel, the generalized energy distance equals twice the squared maximum mean discrepancy (MMD):

Dρ​(P,Q)=2​MMDk2​(P,Q).D_{\rho}(P,Q)=2\,\mathrm{MMD}_{k}^{2}(P,Q).

Second, the MMD is the distance between the kernel mean embeddings μP,μQ\mu_{P},\mu_{Q} of the two distributions in the RKHS ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} (Lemma 4 in Gretton et al. [13]):

MMDk​(P,Q)=‖μP−μQ‖ℋk,\mathrm{MMD}_{k}(P,Q)=\|\mu_{P}-\mu_{Q}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k}},

where a kernel mean embedding is defined as μP=𝔼Z∼P​[k⁡(Z,⋅)].\mu_{P}={\mathbb{E}}_{Z\sim P}\left[k(Z,\cdot)\right].

The squared Mahalanobis distance is generated by the linear kernel k⁡(z,w)=z⊤​Σ−1​wk(z,w)=z^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}w:

k⁡(z,z)+k⁡(w,w)−2​k​(z,w)=z⊤​Σ−1​z+w⊤​Σ−1​w−2​z⊤​Σ−1​w=‖z−w‖Σ−12.k(z,z)+k(w,w)-2\,k(z,w)=z^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}z+w^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}w-2\,z^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}w=\|z-w\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}.

Its mean embedding is the ordinary mean, μP=𝔼Z∼P​[Z]\mu_{P}={\mathbb{E}}_{Z\sim P}[Z], and the RKHS norm reduces to ∥⋅∥Σ−1\|\cdot\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}. Combining the two facts, the discrepancy collapses to a difference of means:

Dρ​(P,Q)=2​‖𝔼Z∼P​[Z]−𝔼W∼Q​[W]‖Σ−12.D_{\rho}(P,Q)=2\,\bigl\|{\mathbb{E}}_{Z\sim P}[Z]-{\mathbb{E}}_{W\sim Q}[W]\bigr\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}.

∎

Proof of Student-t propriety

For the Student-t potential ℰ⁡(u)=log⁡(1+‖u‖Σ−12){\mathcal{E}}(u)=\log\bigl(1+\|u\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}\bigr), the noise density is

qℰ,c​(u)=1Zℰ​(c)​e−c​ℰ​(u)=1Zℰ​(c)​(1+‖u‖Σ−12)−cq_{{\mathcal{E}},c}(u)\,=\frac{1}{Z_{\mathcal{E}}(c)}\,e^{-c\,{\mathcal{E}}(u)}\,=\,\frac{1}{Z_{\mathcal{E}}(c)}\,(1+\|u\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2})^{-c}

for c∈Λℰ=(d/2,∞)c\in\Lambda_{\mathcal{E}}=(d/2,\infty). Setting u=y−Xu=y-X, the matched kernel score is:

Sρ​(P,y)=𝔼X∼P​[log⁡(1+‖y−X‖Σ−12)]−12​𝔼X,X′​∼iid​P​[log⁡(1+‖X−X′‖Σ−12)].S_{\rho}(P,y)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P}\!\left[\log\bigl(1+\|y-X\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}\bigr)\right]\;-\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{X,X^{\prime}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P}\!\left[\log\bigl(1+\|X-X^{\prime}\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}\bigr)\right]. (39)

For propriety, we follow the same approach as above with the composition rule: with k2​(z,w)=‖z−w‖Σ−12k_{2}(z,w)=\|z-w\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2} CND as above, we have:

ρ⁡(z,w)=log⁡(1+‖z−w‖Σ−12)=φ∘k2,φ⁡(t)=log⁡(1+t).\rho(z,w)\;=\;\log\bigl(1+\|z-w\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}\bigr)\;=\;\varphi\circ k_{2},\quad\varphi(t)=\log(1+t).

φ\varphi is Bernstein: it is smooth and nonnegative on [0,∞)[0,\infty), and φ′​(t)=(1+t)−1\varphi^{\prime}(t)=(1+t)^{-1} is completely monotone, since (−1)n​φ(n+1)​(t)=n!​(1+t)−(n+1)≥0(-1)^{n}\varphi^{(n+1)}(t)=n!\,(1+t)^{-(n+1)}\geq 0. Thus ρ\rho is CND by the composition rule, and following Theorem 4 in Gneiting and Raftery [12], the matched kernel score (Eq. 39) is proper.

∎

For strict propriety, we again apply Theorem 5 in Gneiting and Raftery [12] exactly as for the Mahalanobis energy score. For T⁡(z)=L​zT(z)=Lz:

log⁡(1+‖z−w‖Σ−12)=ψ⁡(‖T⁡(z)−T⁡(w)‖22),ψ⁡(t)=log⁡(1+t),\log\bigl(1+\|z-w\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}\bigr)=\psi\left(\|T(z)-T(w)\|_{2}^{2}\right),\quad\psi(t)=\log(1+t),

with ψ\psi continuous on [0,∞)[0,\infty) and ψ′\psi^{\prime} completely monotone and not constant, as verified above; unlike for ψ⁡(t)=tβ/2\psi(t)=t^{\beta/2}, no parameter restriction arises.

Strict propriety moment restriction for Student-t

In the Student-t case, the general pairwise moment requirement in Prop. 4.2 reduces to the explicit logarithmic moment condition stated in Cor. 4.4.

Using ρ⁡(z,w)=ψ⁡(‖T⁡(z)−T⁡(w)‖22)\rho(z,w)=\psi\left(\|T(z)-T(w)\|_{2}^{2}\right) as above, Theorem 5 in Gneiting and Raftery [12] gives strict propriety for distributions PP with finite pairwise moment 𝔼Z,Z′​∼iid​P​[ρ⁡(Z,Z′)]<∞{\mathbb{E}}_{Z,Z^{\prime}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P}\left[\rho(Z,Z^{\prime})\right]<\infty. Since ρ⁡(z,z′)=ℰ⁡(z−z′)\rho(z,z^{\prime})={\mathcal{E}}(z-z^{\prime}), this pairwise condition is equivalent to 𝔼Z,Z′​∼iid​P​[ℰ⁡(Z−Z′)]<∞{\mathbb{E}}_{Z,Z^{\prime}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P}\left[{\mathcal{E}}(Z-Z^{\prime})\right]<\infty. We show below that this is equivalent to the stated condition 𝔼Z∼P​[ℰ​(Z)]<∞{\mathbb{E}}_{Z\sim P}\left[{\mathcal{E}}(Z)\right]<\infty.

For any u,v∈ℝdu,v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the triangle inequality and (a+b)2≤2​a2+2​b2(a+b)^{2}\leq 2a^{2}+2b^{2} give 1+‖u+v‖Σ−12≤4​(1+‖u‖Σ−12)​(1+‖v‖Σ−12)1+\|u+v\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}\leq 4\left(1+\|u\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}\right)\left(1+\|v\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}\right), hence

ℰ⁡(u+v)≤ℰ⁡(u)+ℰ⁡(v)+2​log⁡2.{\mathcal{E}}(u+v)\leq{\mathcal{E}}(u)+{\mathcal{E}}(v)+2\log 2.

Taking u=zu=z, v=−z′v=-z^{\prime} (with ℰ{\mathcal{E}} even) gives ρ⁡(z,z′)≤ℰ⁡(z)+ℰ⁡(z′)+2​log⁡2\rho(z,z^{\prime})\leq{\mathcal{E}}(z)+{\mathcal{E}}(z^{\prime})+2\log 2, so 𝔼Z∼P​[ℰ​(Z)]<∞{\mathbb{E}}_{Z\sim P}\left[{\mathcal{E}}(Z)\right]<\infty implies 𝔼Z,Z′​∼iid​P​[ρ⁡(Z,Z′)]<∞{\mathbb{E}}_{Z,Z^{\prime}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P}\left[\rho(Z,Z^{\prime})\right]<\infty. On the other hand, taking u=z−z′u=z-z^{\prime}, v=z′v=z^{\prime} gives

ℰ⁡(z)≤ρ⁡(z,z′)+ℰ⁡(z′)+2​log⁡2.{\mathcal{E}}(z)\leq\rho(z,z^{\prime})+{\mathcal{E}}(z^{\prime})+2\log 2.

For the converse direction, suppose 𝔼Z,Z′​∼iid​P​[ρ⁡(Z,Z′)]<∞{\mathbb{E}}_{Z,Z^{\prime}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P}[\rho(Z,Z^{\prime})]<\infty. By Fubini’s theorem, there exists a fixed z0∈ℝdz_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} such that

𝔼Z∼P​[ρ⁡(Z,z0)]=𝔼Z∼P​[ℰ⁡(Z−z0)]<∞.{\mathbb{E}}_{Z\sim P}[\rho(Z,z_{0})]={\mathbb{E}}_{Z\sim P}[{\mathcal{E}}(Z-z_{0})]<\infty.

Applying the preceding inequality to Z=(Z−z0)+z0Z=(Z-z_{0})+z_{0} gives

𝔼⁡[ℰ⁡(Z)]≤𝔼⁡[ℰ⁡(Z−z0)]+ℰ⁡(z0)+2​log​2<∞.{\mathbb{E}}[{\mathcal{E}}(Z)]\leq{\mathbb{E}}[{\mathcal{E}}(Z-z_{0})]+{\mathcal{E}}(z_{0})+2\log 2<\infty.

Thus 𝔼Z,Z′​∼iid​P​[ρ⁡(Z,Z′)]<∞{\mathbb{E}}_{Z,Z^{\prime}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P}\left[\rho(Z,Z^{\prime})\right]<\infty also implies 𝔼Z∼P​[ℰ​(Z)]<∞{\mathbb{E}}_{Z\sim P}\left[{\mathcal{E}}(Z)\right]<\infty.

∎

Verification of the assumptions (A1)-(A4) for Student-t

Since ∇ℰ\nabla{\mathcal{E}} is bounded, (A2)–(A4) hold for every data distribution pp; we verify this below.

For the Student-t potential ℰ⁡(u)=log⁡(1+‖u‖Σ−12){\mathcal{E}}(u)=\log(1+\|u\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}), (A1) is exactly the stated restriction c>d/2c>d/2. Furthermore, the gradient satisfies

∥∇ℰ(u)∥=2​‖Σ−1​u‖1+‖u‖Σ−12≤2∥Σ−1/2∥op‖u‖Σ−11+‖u‖Σ−12≤∥Σ−1/2∥op.\|\nabla{\mathcal{E}}(u)\|=\frac{2\|\Sigma^{-1}u\|}{1+\|u\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}}\leq 2\|\Sigma^{-1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\frac{\|u\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}}{1+\|u\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}}\leq\|\Sigma^{-1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}.

Thus ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is smooth and has bounded gradient, which gives (A3) and (A4) for every data distribution.

It remains to check (A2). Since qℰ,c≤Zℰ​(c)−1q_{{\mathcal{E}},c}\leq Z_{\mathcal{E}}(c)^{-1} and ∇qℰ,c=−cqℰ,c∇ℰ\nabla q_{{\mathcal{E}},c}=-c\,q_{{\mathcal{E}},c}\nabla{\mathcal{E}}, the gradient of the noise density is also bounded by a constant CC. By the mean-value theorem, the difference quotients of the noise density in any coordinate direction eie_{i} then satisfy, for all xx and all h≠0h\neq 0:

|qℰ,c​(y+h​ei−x)−qℰ,c​(y−x)h|≤C,\left|\frac{q_{{\mathcal{E}},c}(y+he_{i}-x)-q_{{\mathcal{E}},c}(y-x)}{h}\right|\;\leq\;C,

and the constant CC is integrable under any data distribution pp. Now, (A2) asserts that the generalized Tweedie formula (Eq. 4) holds at yy, and the Stein score is given by sm​(y)=∇y​log​m​(y)=∇m​(y)/m⁡(y)s_{m}(y)=\nabla_{y}\log m(y)=\nabla m(y)/m(y). We can thus exchange the gradient with the integral in the convolution by dominated convergence:

∇m(y)=∇y∫qℰ,c(y−x)p(x)dx=∫∇qℰ,c(y−x)p(x)dx.\nabla m(y)=\nabla_{y}\int q_{{\mathcal{E}},c}(y-x)\,p(x)\,dx=\int\nabla q_{{\mathcal{E}},c}(y-x)\,p(x)\,dx.

Dividing the result by m⁡(y)m(y) and using Bayes’ rule gives:

sm​(y)=1m⁡(y)​∫∇qℰ,c​(y−x)​p​(x)​𝑑x=𝔼⁡[∇log⁡qℰ,c​(y−X)∣Y=y],s_{m}(y)=\frac{1}{m(y)}\int\nabla q_{{\mathcal{E}},c}(y-x)p(x)\,dx={\mathbb{E}}\left[\nabla\log q_{{\mathcal{E}},c}(y-X)\mid Y=y\right],

which is (A2).

A.4 Appendix for Score Estimation

A.4.1 Bias-Variance decomposition of the Monte Carlo Score estimator

Let

hη​(y,x)=−λ​Σ−1​‖y−x‖Σ−1β−2​(y−x)h_{\eta}(y,x)=-\lambda\Sigma^{-1}\|y-x\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{\beta-2}(y-x) (40)

be the clean-conditioned score and

s^N​(y)=1N​∑i=1Nhη​(y,X(i)),\widehat{s}_{N}(y)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}h_{\eta}(y,X^{(i)}),

where X(i)∼iidPθ(⋅∣y)X^{(i)}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y) for i=1,…,Ni=1,\ldots,N. The conditional error separates exactly as

𝔼X(i)∼iidPθ(⋅∣y)[∥s^N(y)−sm(y)∥22]\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{X^{(i)}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y)}\!\left[\|\widehat{s}_{N}(y)-s_{m}(y)\|_{2}^{2}\right] =‖𝔼X∼Pθ(⋅∣y)[hη(y,X)]−sm(y)‖22\displaystyle=\left\|{\mathbb{E}}_{X\sim P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y)}[h_{\eta}(y,X)]-s_{m}(y)\right\|_{2}^{2} (41)
+1NtrCovX∼Pθ(⋅∣y)(hη(y,X)).\displaystyle+\frac{1}{N}\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Cov}_{X\sim P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y)}(h_{\eta}(y,X)).

To see this, let μθ(y)=𝔼X∼Pθ(⋅∣y)[hη(y,X)]\mu_{\theta}(y)={\mathbb{E}}_{X\sim P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y)}[h_{\eta}(y,X)]. Conditional i.i.d. sampling gives

𝔼X(i)∼iidPθ(⋅∣y)[s^N(y)]=μθ(y){\mathbb{E}}_{X^{(i)}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y)}[\widehat{s}_{N}(y)]=\mu_{\theta}(y)

and

CovX(i)∼iidPθ(⋅∣y)(s^N(y))=1NCovX∼Pθ(⋅∣y)(hη(y,X)).\operatorname{Cov}_{X^{(i)}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y)}(\widehat{s}_{N}(y))=\tfrac{1}{N}\operatorname{Cov}_{X\sim P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y)}(h_{\eta}(y,X)).

Expanding the squared error around μθ​(y)\mu_{\theta}(y) gives

𝔼X(i)∼iidPθ(⋅∣y)[∥s^N(y)−sm(y)∥22]\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{X^{(i)}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y)}\!\left[\|\widehat{s}_{N}(y)-s_{m}(y)\|_{2}^{2}\right]
=𝔼X(i)∼iidPθ(⋅∣y)[∥s^N(y)−μθ(y)∥22]+∥μθ(y)−sm(y)∥22\displaystyle\quad={\mathbb{E}}_{X^{(i)}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y)}\!\Big[\|\widehat{s}_{N}(y)-\mu_{\theta}(y)\|_{2}^{2}\Big]+\|\mu_{\theta}(y)-s_{m}(y)\|_{2}^{2}
+2𝔼X(i)∼iidPθ(⋅∣y)[(s^N(y)−μθ(y))⊤(μθ(y)−sm(y))]\displaystyle\qquad\quad+2{\mathbb{E}}_{X^{(i)}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y)}\!\Big[(\widehat{s}_{N}(y)-\mu_{\theta}(y))^{\top}(\mu_{\theta}(y)-s_{m}(y))\Big]
=trCovX(i)∼iidPθ(⋅∣y)(s^N(y))+∥μθ(y)−sm(y)∥22\displaystyle\quad=\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Cov}_{X^{(i)}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y)}(\widehat{s}_{N}(y))+\|\mu_{\theta}(y)-s_{m}(y)\|_{2}^{2}
+2​(𝔼X(i)∼iidPθ(⋅∣y)[s^N(y)]−μθ(y))⊤⏟=μθ​(y)−μθ​(y)=0​(μθ​(y)−sm​(y))\displaystyle\qquad\quad+2\underbrace{\left({\mathbb{E}}_{X^{(i)}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y)}[\widehat{s}_{N}(y)]-\mu_{\theta}(y)\right)^{\top}}_{=\mu_{\theta}(y)-\mu_{\theta}(y)=0}(\mu_{\theta}(y)-s_{m}(y))
=∥μθ(y)−sm(y)∥22+1NtrCovX∼Pθ(⋅∣y)(hη(y,X)).\displaystyle\quad=\|\mu_{\theta}(y)-s_{m}(y)\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{N}\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Cov}_{X\sim P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y)}(h_{\eta}(y,X)).

∎

The first term is the squared bias from the learned posterior and does not depend on NN. The second term is posterior Monte Carlo variance and decays as 1/N1/N. It requires β>1−d/2\beta>1-d/2: ‖hη​(y,x)‖22\|h_{\eta}(y,x)\|_{2}^{2} scales as ‖y−x‖22​(β−1)\|y-x\|_{2}^{2(\beta-1)} near x=yx=y, hence the covariance can be infinite in 1 dimension.

A.4.2 Empirical Score Comparisons

Estimators and evaluation.

As a reminder, we compare three approaches:

  • •

    the posterior route uses the identity directly in conjunction with samples from the denoising posterior, averaging the known clean-conditioned score hη​(y,X)h_{\eta}(y,X) (Eq. 40) over 192192 draws.

  • •

    ET-DSM learns a neural network sθ​(y,η)s_{\theta}(y,\eta) by regressing against hη​(Y,X)h_{\eta}(Y,X) using clean–noisy pairs.

  • •

    Hyvärinen score matching uses a similar neural architecture but trains on noisy data alone. While in principle it does not require the noise parameters as an input (cf. Sec. 5.2), we condition the network on the noise parameters to reuse it across experiments (i.e., not have to retrain it in each setting).

Noise magnitude.

All comparisons in this appendix use the five-parameter generalized Gaussian noise of Sec. 5.1, η=(β,λ,σ,u,v)\eta=(\beta,\lambda,\sigma,u,v) with Σ=σ2​S​(u,v)\Sigma=\sigma^{2}S(u,v), on the two-dimensional Eight-Gaussians data. The scale σ\sigma alone does not determine how far the noise displaces an observation, since the displacement also depends on β\beta and λ\lambda. To compare parameter combinations at equal noise strength, we use the per-coordinate root mean square (RMS) displacement of a noise draw rηr_{\eta}:

cβ,d2=β2/β​Γ​((d+2)/β)d​Γ​(d/β),ρ=cβ,dσ,rη=ρλ−1/β,c_{\beta,d}^{2}=\frac{\beta^{2/\beta}\,\Gamma((d+2)/\beta)}{d\,\Gamma(d/\beta)},\qquad\rho=c_{\beta,d}\,\sigma,\qquad r_{\eta}=\rho\,\lambda^{-1/\beta}, (42)

where dd is the ambient dimension, here d=2d=2. We call ρ\rho, the value of rηr_{\eta} at λ=1\lambda=1, the reference RMS; it is the magnitude coordinate on which the five-parameter models are conditioned (App. A.8). In the experimental appendices and figures, ρ\rho denotes this scalar, unrelated to the kernel discrepancy of Sec. 4, as should be apparent from context.

Noise-parameter combinations and ground truth.

The sweeps of Table 1 vary one parameter at a time around the default combination (β,λ,σ,u,v)=(1.4, 1.8, 0.45, 0, 0.6)(\beta,\lambda,\sigma,u,v)=(1.4,\,1.8,\,0.45,\,0,\,0.6): β∈{1.3,1.5,1.75,2}\beta\in\{1.3,1.5,1.75,2\}, λ∈{1,1.4,1.8,2.5}\lambda\in\{1,1.4,1.8,2.5\}, σ∈{0.1,0.25,0.45,0.75}\sigma\in\{0.1,0.25,0.45,0.75\}, and u,v∈{−0.6,−0.3,0,0.3,0.6}u,v\in\{-0.6,-0.3,0,0.3,0.6\}, where the other coordinate is held at 00 while uu or vv is swept. All combinations are specified through the reference RMS ρ\rho and converted to σ\sigma at the combination’s β\beta; the β\beta sweep therefore holds ρ=0.570\rho=0.570 fixed while the tail shape changes, and the magnitude sweep ρ∈{0.13,0.32,0.57,0.95}\rho\in\{0.13,0.32,0.57,0.95\} is reported as σ∈{0.1,0.25,0.45,0.75}\sigma\in\{0.1,0.25,0.45,0.75\} at β=1.4\beta=1.4. In total there are 2222 parameter combinations with 192192 noisy observations each.

When the noise is Gaussian, the noised score is analytic. This is not the case for generalized Gaussian noise, so to obtain a high-quality reference for evaluation we construct a numerical ground truth by importance sampling from the clean data distribution: a bank of 160,000160{,}000 clean particles is reweighted by the generalized Gaussian likelihood at the observation, and the ground-truth score is the weighted average of the clean-conditioned score hηh_{\eta} (Eq. 40) over the bank. The bank is split into two independent halves. The ground truth is the average of the two half-bank estimates, and the NMSE between the halves, reported as the ground-truth disagreement in Table 1, measures the precision of the ground truth itself. The posterior route averages 192192 posterior draws per observation. The direct estimators are evaluated at the same parameter combinations with the same number of observations and the same bank size, but with separately generated observations and ground truths, so Table 6 lists the ground-truth precision of each evaluation.

Accuracy across the sweeps.

Figure 3 shows NMSE and cosine similarity at every parameter combination, which is the data behind the means presented in Table 1 in the main text. ET-DSM has the lowest NMSE in every sweep, followed by Hyvärinen score matching and then the posterior route. The three estimators agree in direction and magnitude: the sweep-mean cosine similarity exceeds 0.950.95 for every estimator, and the norm ratios lie within a few percent of one (Table 4). The largest error of the posterior route occurs at the smallest scale σ=0.1\sigma=0.1, where the importance-sampled ground truth is also least precise (Table 6): as the noise shrinks, the posterior concentrates on few bank particles, the effective sample size drops, and the two half-bank estimates disagree by an NMSE far larger than at the other combinations. As noted in the main text, while the two direct estimators were ensured to be well-trained in order for a maximally rigorous comparison (see Training of the direct estimators below), no such procedure was done for the posterior, so its slightly lower accuracy might be due to undertraining.

We can also compare the posterior model draws and the importance posterior directly. Table 5 reports the error of the posterior mean, the ratio of the posterior covariance traces, the total variation distance between the assignments of posterior mass to the nearest mixture centers, and the energy distance between the two posteriors, together with its excess over the energy distance between two independent resamples of the importance posterior. The results show that the learned posterior is centered and assigns modes correctly; its remaining error is a mild overdispersion (trace ratio 1.041.04–1.111.11), consistent with the nonzero score NMSE that the posterior route retains as N→∞N\to\infty (Table 9) and pointing to mild undertraining.

Noise-magnitude range.

The sweeps above span less than one decade of noise magnitude. Figure 4 supplements this by evaluating the posterior route over three decades, using the isotropic Gaussian and generalized Gaussian noise with the remaining parameters fixed. Cosine similarity dips at intermediate magnitudes, with the dip confined to the observations whose ground-truth score has below-median norm: where the ground-truth score is small, a small absolute error produces a large angular error, and the score NMSE in this region stays at or below 0.0100.010. Replacing the learned posterior by the exact one (analytic for Gaussian noise, importance-sampled for generalized Gaussian noise) reproduces the dip (Table 7), which places the responsibility in the Monte Carlo estimate at those observations rather than in the learned model. At the smallest magnitudes, shaded gray, the half-bank ground-truth NMSE exceeds 0.010.01 and the comparison is thus limited by the ground truth.

Training of the direct estimators.

ET-DSM and Hyvärinen score matching share the architecture, initialization, and data stream described in App. A.8. With the factor 12\tfrac{1}{2} included by convention, the objectives at a fixed parameter combination η\eta are

Dη​(θ)\displaystyle D_{\eta}(\theta) =12​ℒET​-​DSM​(θ,η),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ET\text{-}DSM}}(\theta;\eta),
Hη​(θ)\displaystyle H_{\eta}(\theta) =𝔼Y∼mη​[12​‖sθ​(Y,η)‖22+divY⁡sθ​(Y,η)],\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m_{\eta}}[\tfrac{1}{2}\|s_{\theta}(Y,\eta)\|_{2}^{2}+\operatorname{div}_{Y}s_{\theta}(Y,\eta)], (43)

with ℒET​-​DSM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ET\text{-}DSM}} from Eq. 25 and mη=p∗qηm_{\eta}=p*q_{\eta} the noisy marginal.

Each minibatch draws one parameter combination from the law used to train the five-parameter Eight-Gaussians posterior (App. A.8). The objectives are averaged over combinations with the weight rη2r_{\eta}^{2} in order for the small-noise cases not to dominate the loss.

Both objectives have known population minima, so we can ensure that the training has converged. Let sη=∇log⁡mηs_{\eta}=\nabla\log m_{\eta} be the noisy score, Iη=𝔼Y∼mη​[‖sη​(Y)‖22]I_{\eta}={\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m_{\eta}}[\|s_{\eta}(Y)\|_{2}^{2}] its expected squared norm, and Cη=𝔼X∼p,Y∼qη(⋅∣X)[∥hη(Y,X)∥22]C_{\eta}={\mathbb{E}}_{X\sim p,\,Y\sim q_{\eta}(\cdot\mid X)}[\|h_{\eta}(Y,X)\|_{2}^{2}] that of the clean-conditioned score (Eq. 40). Under the integration-by-parts conditions of score matching, we get [15; 45]:

Hη∗\displaystyle H_{\eta}^{*} =−Iη/2,Dη∗=(Cη−Iη)/2,\displaystyle=-I_{\eta}/2,\qquad D_{\eta}^{*}=(C_{\eta}-I_{\eta})/2, (44)
Hη​(θ)−Hη∗\displaystyle H_{\eta}(\theta)-H_{\eta}^{*} =Dη​(θ)−Dη∗=12​𝔼Y∼mη​[‖sθ​(Y,η)−sη​(Y)‖22],\displaystyle=D_{\eta}(\theta)-D_{\eta}^{*}=\tfrac{1}{2}{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m_{\eta}}[\|s_{\theta}(Y,\eta)-s_{\eta}(Y)\|_{2}^{2}],

so both objectives exceed their minima by half the mean squared score error, and this excess divided by Iη/2I_{\eta}/2 is the score NMSE at that combination. For the two-dimensional generalized Gaussian,

Cη=λ2​tr⁡(S−1)2​σ2​(βλ)2−2/β​1Γ⁡(2/β),C_{\eta}=\frac{\lambda^{2}\operatorname{tr}(S^{-1})}{2\sigma^{2}}\left(\frac{\beta}{\lambda}\right)^{2-2/\beta}\frac{1}{\Gamma(2/\beta)},

while IηI_{\eta} is estimated on the validation set from the inner product of the two half-bank ground-truth scores. Validation is evaluated every 2,0002{,}000 updates. We can thus evaluate the theoretical minima from Eq. 44 and perform the same weighted average as for the loss to obtain a loss floor in Fig. 5. The validation curves settle near their floors, and the final relative gaps are between 1%1\% and 5%5\% (Table 8), so (at least at the chosen validation parameter values) the two network sets are near-optimally trained. The minibatch training losses are variable as each minibatch draws a new parameter combination with its own population minimum.

Compute Budgets.

The three estimators share the clean distribution and the noise-parameter law above. Each direct estimation network is trained on 327.68327.68 million fresh clean–noisy pairs under 80,00080{,}000 draws of the parameter combination; the posterior model, which is also the model behind the diffusion experiments of App. A.6.1, was trained on 22.422.4 billion pairs under 560,000560{,}000 draws of the parameter combination. Naturally, the networks are not comparable, as the direct estimation networks estimate the score alone, while we use the same posterior network for all three presented applications. For the posterior route, Eq. 41 separates the error at an observation into the squared bias of the learned posterior, which additional draws do not reduce, and the Monte Carlo variance, which decays as 1/N1/N. Table 9 holds the two trained posteriors (i.e., two random seeds) fixed at the default parameter combination and measures the error over nine posterior sample budgets, with ten repetitions per model.

Fitting a+b/Na+b/N jointly over the nine posterior sample budgets gives an NMSE floor a=0.023a=0.023 and slope b=1.41b=1.41. The two models have nearly identical slopes (1.4091.409 and 1.4061.406) and different floors (0.0170.017 and 0.0290.029), matching the separation in Eq. 41 between posterior variance and per-model approximation bias (which differs between model instances).

Clean score fields.

Fig. 6 presents the approximate clean score field obtained via the Richardson extrapolation (Sec. 5.1) and the analytic ground truth. We use two MLP-based Engression posteriors [35], conditioned on log⁡σ\log\sigma and trained over σ∈[0.01,10]\sigma\in[0.01,10], for isotropic Gaussian (β,λ)=(2,1)(\beta,\lambda)=(2,1) and generalized Gaussian (β,λ)=(1.4,1.8)(\beta,\lambda)=(1.4,1.8) noise. The Richardson pair (ε1,ε2)(\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2}) is the adjacent pair from that training-range noise grid with the lowest clean-score MSE. As the models were not trained to target the small-noise regime, the comparison is mostly qualitative.

A.4.3 Derivations

Small-noise limit.

First, Cor. 4.3 holds for any choice of parameters (β,λ,Σ)(\beta,\lambda,\Sigma). The Mahalanobis metric reduces to the Euclidean one in whitened coordinates:

∥u∥βΣ−1=∥Σ−1/2u∥2β.\|u\|^{\beta}_{\Sigma^{-1}}=\|\Sigma^{-1/2}u\|_{2}^{\beta}.

Now write Σ=ε2​Σ0\Sigma=\varepsilon^{2}\Sigma_{0}. For the generalized Gaussian distribution,

qε(u)∝exp(−λβ​εβ∥Σ0−1/2u∥2β),q_{\varepsilon}(u)\ \propto\ \exp\Big(-\frac{\lambda}{\beta~\varepsilon^{\beta}}~\|\Sigma_{0}^{-1/2}u\|_{2}^{\beta}\Big), (45)

and ∥u∥Σ−1=ε−1∥Σ0−1/2u∥2\|u\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}=\varepsilon^{-1}\|\Sigma_{0}^{-1/2}u\|_{2}. Let Pε(⋅∣Y=y)P_{\varepsilon}(\cdot\mid Y=y) denote the posterior induced by the clean density pp and noising density qεq_{\varepsilon}, and let mε=p∗qεm_{\varepsilon}=p*q_{\varepsilon}. The Energy-Tweedie identity gives

smε(y)=−λβ1εβ∇yPD𝔼X∼Pε(⋅∣Y=y)[∥Σ0−1/2(X−y)∥2β].s_{m_{\varepsilon}}(y)=-\frac{\lambda}{\beta}\;\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{\beta}}\nabla^{\mathrm{PD}}_{y}~{\mathbb{E}}_{X\sim P_{\varepsilon}(\cdot\mid Y=y)}[\|\Sigma_{0}^{-1/2}(X-y)\|_{2}^{\beta}]. (46)

This can be approximated via Monte Carlo samples from a trained posterior X(k)∼P^θ,ε(⋅∣Y=y)X^{(k)}\sim\widehat{P}_{\theta,\varepsilon}(\cdot\mid Y=y):

s^ε(y)=−λβ​εβ∇yPD1K∑k=1K‖Σ0−1/2(X(k)−y)‖2β,\widehat{s}_{\varepsilon}(y)=-\frac{\lambda}{\beta~\varepsilon^{\beta}}\nabla_{y}^{\mathrm{PD}}\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left\|\Sigma_{0}^{-1/2}\left(X^{(k)}-y\right)\right\|_{2}^{\beta}, (47)

(or equivalently using Eq. 23 if one does not wish to use automatic differentiation).

For the limiting clean score, assume p⁡(y)>0p(y)>0, pp is differentiable in a neighborhood of yy, and the scaled kernels qεq_{\varepsilon} form an approximate identity for both pp and ∇p\nabla p at yy:

(p∗qε)(y)→p(y),(∇p∗qε)(y)→∇p(y).(p*q_{\varepsilon})(y)\to p(y),\qquad(\nabla p*q_{\varepsilon})(y)\to\nabla p(y).

A basic sufficient condition is continuity of pp and ∇p\nabla p near yy, together with a dominated-convergence condition allowing convolution with the generalized-Gaussian tails. Under these conditions,

∇ymε(y)=∇y(p∗qε)(y)=(∇p∗qε)(y)→∇p(y),\nabla_{y}m_{\varepsilon}(y)=\nabla_{y}(p*q_{\varepsilon})(y)=(\nabla p*q_{\varepsilon})(y)\to\nabla p(y),

while mε​(y)→p⁡(y)>0m_{\varepsilon}(y)\to p(y)>0. Therefore

smε​(y)=∇y​log​mε​(y)=∇ymε​(y)mε​(y)⟶∇yp​(y)p⁡(y)=∇y​log​p​(y).s_{m_{\varepsilon}}(y)=\nabla_{y}\log m_{\varepsilon}(y)=\frac{\nabla_{y}m_{\varepsilon}(y)}{m_{\varepsilon}(y)}\longrightarrow\frac{\nabla_{y}p(y)}{p(y)}=\nabla_{y}\log p(y).

Combining this with Eq. 46 gives the small-noise clean-score limit used in Sec. 5.1. The stronger 𝒞7{\mathcal{C}}^{7} condition used for the Richardson expansion below should be read together with this dominated-convergence condition when the expansion is exchanged with the integral.

Richardson error order.

The Richardson extrapolation estimator (Eq. 26) is defined for two small ε1,ε2\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2} such that ε1=aε,ε2=bε,a,b>0,a≠b,ε≪1\varepsilon_{1}=a\varepsilon,\varepsilon_{2}=b\varepsilon,~~a,b>0,a\neq b,\varepsilon\ll 1 and assuming the same regularity and p∈𝒞7p\in{\mathcal{C}}^{7} around yy.

qε(u)∝exp(−λβ​εβ∥Σ0−1/2u∥2β)q_{\varepsilon}(u)\ \propto\ \exp\Big(-\frac{\lambda}{\beta~\varepsilon^{\beta}}~\|\Sigma_{0}^{-1/2}u\|_{2}^{\beta}\Big)

A.5 Appendix for Parameter Estimation

A.5.1 Theoretical Appendix

This subsection collects the formal results supporting the estimation criterion in Sec. 5.2, specialized to the generalized Gaussian case.

For reference, the population criterion from Eq. 28 can be written as

J0​(β,λ,Σ)=𝔼Y∼m​[‖sm​(Y)−λ​G​(Y,β,Σ)‖22],J_{0}(\beta,\lambda,\Sigma)={\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}\left[\left\|s_{m}(Y)-\lambda G(Y;\beta,\Sigma)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (49)

where

G(Y;β,Σ)=−1β∇YPDESΣ−1,β(P(⋅∣Y),Y)G(Y;\beta,\Sigma)=-\frac{1}{\beta}\nabla_{Y}^{\mathrm{PD}}\mathrm{ES}_{\Sigma^{-1},\beta}\big(P(\cdot\mid Y),Y\big)

is the residual field previously defined in Eq. 29.

Throughout this subsection, we adopt the regularity condition discussed in App. A.2.3: 𝔼⁡[‖y−X‖Σ−1β−1∣Y=y]<∞{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\|y-X\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{\beta-1}\mid Y=y\right]<\infty. As discussed there, this condition is satisfied whenever the data density is locally bounded near the observation yy.

The profiled scalar scale is the least-squares coefficient in Eq. 30; when a finite valid set Λ=[λmin,λmax]\Lambda=[\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}] is imposed, the implementation uses ΠΛ​(a)=min⁡{λmax,max⁡{λmin,a}}\Pi_{\Lambda}(a)=\min\{\lambda_{\max},\max\{\lambda_{\min},a\}\}.

Theorem A.1 is the population statement: without a trace constraint, the true parameters are identified only up to the standard elliptical scale equivalence; with Tr⁡(Σ)=d\Tr(\Sigma)=d, the normalized representative is unique. Proposition A.2 turns this population identification into consistency of the plug-in noise-parameter estimator when the auxiliary score estimator and Monte Carlo posterior field are consistent. Corollary A.3 justifies profiling λ\lambda, which is the reduction used by Alg. 1.

Theorem A.1 (Oracle Identifiability of the Noise Parameters)

Let Θ=Δ{(β∈(0,2],λ>0,Σ≻0)}\Theta\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Delta}}{{=}}\{(\beta\in(0,2],\lambda>0,\Sigma\succ 0)\} and let the true parameters of the noising distribution be denoted by θ∗=(β∗,λ∗,Σ∗)\theta^{*}=(\beta^{*},\lambda^{*},\Sigma^{*}). 1) The optimizers under the true posterior P(⋅∣Y)P(\cdot\mid Y) of the population-level objective J0J_{0} in Eq. 49 include the equivalence class

{(β∗,cβ∗/2​λ∗,c​Σ∗)∣c∈ℝ+}.\{(\beta^{*},c^{\beta^{*}/2}\,\lambda^{*},c\,\Sigma^{*})\mid c\in\mathbb{R}^{+}\}.

In particular,

J0​(β∗,cβ∗/2​λ∗,c​Σ∗)=J0​(β∗,λ∗,Σ∗)≡0,∀c∈ℝ+.J_{0}(\beta^{*},c^{\beta^{*}/2}\,\lambda^{*},c\,\Sigma^{*})=J_{0}(\beta^{*},\lambda^{*},\Sigma^{*})\equiv 0,~\forall c\in\mathbb{R}^{+}.

2) Assume the true equivalence class is represented by the normalized tuple θ∗=(β∗,λ∗,Σ∗)\theta^{*}=(\beta^{*},\lambda^{*},\Sigma^{*}) with

Tr⁡(Σ∗)=d,\Tr(\Sigma^{*})=d,

that is Θd={(β,λ,Σ):β∈(0,2],λ>0,Σ≻0,Tr(Σ)=d}\Theta_{d}=\{(\beta,\lambda,\Sigma):\beta\in(0,2],\lambda>0,\Sigma\succ 0,\operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma)=d\}. Further, assume convolution identifiability for the clean data distribution pp: for every θ∈Θd\theta\in\Theta_{d}, if (p∗fθ)​(y)=0(p*f_{\theta})(y)=0 for mm-a.e. yy, then fθ​(u)=0f_{\theta}(u)=0 for (Lebesgue-)a.e. uu. Here,

fθ=qθ∗​(∇uΦθ​(u)−∇uΦθ∗​(u)),Φθ​(u)=Δλβ​‖u‖Σ−1β,f_{\theta}=q_{\theta^{*}}(\nabla_{u}\Phi_{\theta}(u)-\nabla_{u}\Phi_{\theta^{*}}(u)),\qquad\Phi_{\theta}(u)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Delta}}{{=}}\frac{\lambda}{\beta}\|u\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{\beta},

where Φθ=c​ℰ=λβ​ℰ\Phi_{\theta}=c{\mathcal{E}}=\frac{\lambda}{\beta}\,{\mathcal{E}}, and ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is the potential of the generalized Gaussian.

Then, the restricted population optimization problem with Tr⁡(Σ)=d\Tr(\Sigma)=d admits a unique restricted optimizer, namely the representative parameter tuple (β∗,λ∗,Σ∗)(\beta^{*},\lambda^{*},\Sigma^{*}).

The proof is given in App. A.5.3. It first records the scale orbit of equivalent generalized-Gaussian parameterizations and then uses the trace constraint plus convolution identifiability to pin down the normalized representative.

Proposition A.2 (Consistency of the Plug-in Estimator)

Let θ=(β,λ,Σ)\theta=(\beta,\lambda,\Sigma) denote the noise parameters and let Θ⊂Θd\Theta\subset\Theta_{d} be a compact subset of the restricted parameter space containing the true parameter tuple θ∗=(β∗,λ∗,Σ∗)\theta^{*}=(\beta^{*},\lambda^{*},\Sigma^{*}). Assume that the posterior term in the criterion is correctly specified, i.e., it uses P(⋅∣Y=y)P(\cdot\mid Y=y), and use Gβ,Σ​(y)G_{\beta,\Sigma}(y) defined in Eq. 29. For Y1,…,Yn​∼iid​mY_{1},\ldots,Y_{n}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}m, let

Jn​(θ)=Δ1n​∑i=1n‖sm​(Yi)−λ​Gβ,Σ​(Yi)‖22, and​J^n​(θ)=Δ1n​∑i=1n‖s^m,n​(Yi)−λ​Gβ,Σ​(Yi)‖22J_{n}(\theta)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Delta}}{{=}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\|s_{m}(Y_{i})-\lambda G_{\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2}\quad\text{, and}~\widehat{J}_{n}(\theta)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Delta}}{{=}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\|\widehat{s}_{m,n}(Y_{i})-\lambda G_{\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2}

be the sample-based versions of the population criterion J0J_{0} in Eq. 49 based on the oracle and the plug-in score estimator s^m,n\widehat{s}_{m,n}, respectively. Assume J0J_{0} is continuous on Θ\Theta, and that JnJ_{n} is uniformly consistent:

supθ∈Θ|Jn​(θ)−J0​(θ)|→P0.\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left|J_{n}(\theta)-J_{0}(\theta)\right|\stackrel{{\scriptstyle P}}{{\rightarrow}}0.

For the score terms, assume that s^m,n\widehat{s}_{m,n} is empirically L2L_{2}-consistent on the evaluation sample:

1n​∑i=1n‖s^m,n​(Yi)−sm​(Yi)‖22=op​(1),\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\|\widehat{s}_{m,n}(Y_{i})-s_{m}(Y_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2}=o_{p}(1),

and the oracle residual w.r.t. the Energy-Tweedie term is empirically bounded in the second moment:

1n​∑i=1nsupθ∈Θ‖sm​(Yi)−λ​Gβ,Σ​(Yi)‖22=Op​(1).\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left\|s_{m}(Y_{i})-\lambda G_{\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2}=O_{p}(1).

By Theorem A.1, θ∗\theta^{*} is the unique minimizer of J0J_{0} on Θ\Theta, thus if θ^n\widehat{\theta}_{n} is any approximate minimizer satisfying

J^n​(θ^n)≤infθ∈ΘJ^n​(θ)+op​(1),\widehat{J}_{n}(\widehat{\theta}_{n})\leq\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\widehat{J}_{n}(\theta)+o_{p}(1),

then

θ^n→Pθ∗.\widehat{\theta}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle P}}{{\rightarrow}}\theta^{*}.

Now suppose that Gβ,ΣG_{\beta,\Sigma} is replaced by a Monte Carlo estimate G^Kn,β,Σ\widehat{G}_{K_{n},\beta,\Sigma} computed from KnK_{n} posterior samples per evaluation point. If

1n​∑i=1nsupθ∈Θλ2​‖G^Kn,β,Σ​(Yi)−Gβ,Σ​(Yi)‖22=op​(1),\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\lambda^{2}\left\|\widehat{G}_{K_{n},\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})-G_{\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2}=o_{p}(1),

then with the corresponding Monte Carlo criterion:

J^n,KnMC​(β,λ,Σ)=Δ1n​∑i=1n‖s^m,n​(Yi)−λ​G^Kn,β,Σ​(Yi)‖22,\widehat{J}_{n,K_{n}}^{\mathrm{MC}}(\beta,\lambda,\Sigma)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Delta}}{{=}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\|\widehat{s}_{m,n}(Y_{i})-\lambda\widehat{G}_{K_{n},\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2},

the same conclusion holds for its approximate minimizers: θ^n,KnMC→Pθ∗.\widehat{\theta}^{\mathrm{MC}}_{n,K_{n}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle P}}{{\rightarrow}}\theta^{*}.

The proof is given in App. A.5.3.

Corollary A.3 (λ\lambda Profile Closed-Form)

With G⁡(y,β,Σ)G(y;\beta,\Sigma) defined in Eq. 29, for every fixed β\beta and Σ\Sigma with 𝔼Y∼m​[‖G⁡(Y,β,Σ)‖22]>0{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}[\|G(Y;\beta,\Sigma)\|_{2}^{2}]>0, the unconstrained optimizer for λ\lambda in Eq. 49 is given by Eq. 30. If this value is positive, it is also the optimizer under the constraint λ>0\lambda>0; otherwise the constrained infimum is approached as λ↓0\lambda\downarrow 0. For a finite valid interval Λ=[λmin,λmax]\Lambda=[\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}], the constrained optimizer is the projected coefficient ΠΛ​[λ∗​(β,Σ)]\Pi_{\Lambda}[\lambda^{*}(\beta,\Sigma)]. Furthermore, in the Gaussian case this simplifies to:

λ∗​(β=2,Σ)=𝔼Y∼m​[⟨sm​(Y),Σ−1​(𝔼⁡[X∣Y]−Y)⟩]𝔼Y∼m​[‖Σ−1​(𝔼⁡[X∣Y]−Y)‖22],\lambda^{*}(\beta=2,\Sigma)=\frac{{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}\left[\langle s_{m}(Y),\Sigma^{-1}({\mathbb{E}}[X\mid Y]-Y)\rangle\right]}{{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}\left[\|\Sigma^{-1}({\mathbb{E}}[X\mid Y]-Y)\|^{2}_{2}\right]}, (50)

and in the isotropic case Σ=σ2​Id\Sigma=\sigma^{2}I_{d} this further simplifies to:

λ∗​(β=2,σ2​Id)=σ2​𝔼Y∼m​[⟨sm​(Y),𝔼⁡[X∣Y]−Y⟩]𝔼Y∼m​[‖𝔼⁡[X∣Y]−Y‖22].\lambda^{*}(\beta=2,\sigma^{2}I_{d})=\sigma^{2}\,\frac{{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}\left[\langle s_{m}(Y),{\mathbb{E}}[X\mid Y]-Y\rangle\right]}{{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}\left[\|{\mathbb{E}}[X\mid Y]-Y\|^{2}_{2}\right]}. (51)

In words, this is the global least-squares projection coefficient of the noisy score onto the residual field induced by the fixed (β,Σ)(\beta,\Sigma).

The proof is given in App. A.5.3.

The algorithm below combines these ingredients in the form used in the estimation experiment: Σ\Sigma is parameterized with trace normalization, λ\lambda is profiled by Cor. A.3 and projected to the valid interval Λ\Lambda, and the remaining shape parameters are updated by gradient steps on the profiled objective.

A.5.2 Extra Empirical Results

We present the full results of the experiment in Tab. 2 in Tab. 10. To recap: the correctly specified family estimates (β,λ,u,v)(\beta,\lambda,u,v); the Gaussian control fixes β=2\beta=2 while retaining the full learned SPD matrix; the isotropic generalized control fixes u=v=0u=v=0 while estimating (β,λ)(\beta,\lambda); and the isotropic Gaussian control imposes both restrictions. Every family is crossed with the four score/posterior source combinations on the same paired estimation and held-out observations. The truth is (β∗,λ∗,u∗,v∗)=(1.4,1.8,0.25,0.35)(\beta^{*},\lambda^{*},u^{*},v^{*})=(1.4,1.8,0.25,0.35), and all held-out errors use the same oracle noisy score. As in Table 2, the “oracle” score and posterior are the importance-sampled ground truth, and the “learned” score and posterior are the Hyvärinen estimator and the SPD-conditioned Engressor. The values are estimated from 384384 estimation and 384384 held-out observations per noise level, pooled over the three noise levels (totaling 11521152 observations each), with 256256 posterior samples per observation. We generate 5 replicates of the data, each paired with its own trained score estimator (in the learned-score case). For the learned posterior entries, each data replicate is additionally fitted with each of 33 separately trained posterior models. Score estimates and posterior draws are generated once per observation before the fit and held fixed during the optimization, so the plug-in objective is deterministic given the data replicate and the same samples serve every fitted family.

The full table confirms the conclusions of Tab. 2 under every source combination: the correctly specified family has the lowest held-out error and recovers the non-diagonal geometry throughout (‖S^−S⋆‖F=0.0079\|\widehat{S}-S^{\star}\|_{F}=0.0079–0.01180.0118), and the family ordering is identical for all four source combinations. Replacing the oracle score with the learned Hyvärinen score changes MSE by at most 0.00350.0035 at a fixed family and posterior source. The constrained fits again compensate in characteristic ways regardless of the estimator: forcing Gaussian tails keeps the SPD coordinates accurate but lowers λ^\widehat{\lambda} to 1.461.46–1.511.51, while forcing isotropy drags β^\widehat{\beta} down to 1.121.12–1.131.13.

A.5.3 Proofs of Section 5.2

The next few subsections give the proofs for the formal statements above.

Proof of Theorem A.1

∇yPDES(c​Σ)−1,β(P,y)=c−β/2∇yPDESΣ−1,β(P,y),∀y,\nabla_{y}^{\mathrm{PD}}\mathrm{ES}_{(c\Sigma)^{-1},\beta}(P,y)=c^{-\beta/2}\nabla_{y}^{\mathrm{PD}}\mathrm{ES}_{\Sigma^{-1},\beta}(P,y),~~\forall y,

≤2n​∑i=1n‖ei‖2​supθ∈Θ‖ri​(θ)‖2+1n​∑i=1n‖ei‖22.\displaystyle\leq\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|e_{i}\|_{2}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|r_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|e_{i}\|_{2}^{2}.

We have assumed that the plug-in estimator has an empirical L2L_{2}-consistency on the evaluation sample:

1n​∑i=1n‖ei‖22=1n​∑i=1n‖s^m,n​(Yi)−sm​(Yi)‖22=op​(1).\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\|e_{i}\right\|^{2}_{2}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\|\widehat{s}_{m,n}(Y_{i})-s_{m}(Y_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2}=o_{p}(1).

This is an empirical analogue of Fisher-divergence consistency, the latter being common for score-matching estimators [38]. We leave it as a high-level assumption since its verification depends on the exact score estimator, model class, data regularity, and other factors. This means that:

supθ∈Θ|J^n​(θ)−Jn​(θ)|≤2n​∑i=1n‖ei‖2​supθ∈Θ‖ri​(θ)‖2+op​(1).\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left|\widehat{J}_{n}(\theta)-J_{n}(\theta)\right|\leq\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|e_{i}\|_{2}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|r_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}+o_{p}(1).

We can further handle the remaining term by applying the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality again:

2n​∑i=1n‖ei‖2​supθ∈Θ‖ri​(θ)‖2≤2​(1n​∑i=1n‖ei‖22)1/2​(1n​∑i=1nsupθ∈Θ‖ri​(θ)‖22)1/2.\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|e_{i}\|_{2}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|r_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}\leq 2\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|e_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\right)^{1/2}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|r_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}\right)^{1/2}.

So by the same assumption, the first factor is op​(1)o_{p}(1). For the second term, we have assumed that it is empirically bounded in the second moment:

1n​∑i=1nsupθ∈Θ‖sm​(Yi)−λ​Gθ​(Yi)‖22=Op​(1).\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left\|s_{m}(Y_{i})-\lambda G_{\theta}(Y_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2}=O_{p}(1).

Thus, the whole is op​(1)o_{p}(1):

supθ∈Θ|J^n​(θ)−Jn​(θ)|=op​(1).\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left|\widehat{J}_{n}(\theta)-J_{n}(\theta)\right|=o_{p}(1).

By the triangle inequality, we have:

supθ∈Θ|J^n​(θ)−J0​(θ)|≤supθ∈Θ|J^n​(θ)−Jn​(θ)|+supθ∈Θ|Jn​(θ)−J0​(θ)|.\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left|\widehat{J}_{n}(\theta)-J_{0}(\theta)\right|\leq\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left|\widehat{J}_{n}(\theta)-J_{n}(\theta)\right|+\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left|J_{n}(\theta)-J_{0}(\theta)\right|.

The first term is op​(1)o_{p}(1) by the above, and the second term is op​(1)o_{p}(1) by assumption. Hence:

supθ∈Θ|J^n​(θ)−J0​(θ)|=op​(1).\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left|\widehat{J}_{n}(\theta)-J_{0}(\theta)\right|=o_{p}(1).

We will use Theorem 5.7 in Vaart [44] with Mn​(θ)=−J^n​(θ)M_{n}(\theta)=-\widehat{J}_{n}(\theta) and M⁡(θ)=−J0​(θ)M(\theta)=-J_{0}(\theta). First, the last result means:

J^n​(θ^n)≤infθ∈ΘJ^n​(θ)+op​(1)≤J^n​(θ∗)+op​(1).\widehat{J}_{n}(\widehat{\theta}_{n})\leq\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\widehat{J}_{n}(\theta)+o_{p}(1)\leq\widehat{J}_{n}(\theta^{*})+o_{p}(1).

Second: let

Aε={θ∈Θ:d⁡(θ,θ∗)≥ε}.A_{\varepsilon}=\left\{\theta\in\Theta:d\left(\theta,\theta^{*}\right)\geq\varepsilon\right\}.

As Θ\Theta is assumed compact and J0J_{0} is assumed continuous, J0J_{0} attains its minimum on AεA_{\varepsilon}. Theorem A.1 already gives θ∗\theta^{*} as the unique minimizer on the compact set Θ\Theta. Hence:

infθ∈AεJ0​(θ)>J0​(θ∗).\inf_{\theta\in A_{\varepsilon}}J_{0}(\theta)>J_{0}(\theta^{*}).

Thus, by Theorem 5.7 in Vaart [44], we have that

θ^n→Pθ∗.\widehat{\theta}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle P}}{{\rightarrow}}\theta^{*}.
Monte Carlo extension:

We denote the Monte Carlo plug-in for Gβ,ΣG_{\beta,\Sigma} as:

G^Kn,β,Σ​(Yi)=ΔΣ−1​1Kn​∑k=1Kn‖Xi,k−Yi‖Σ−1β−2​(Xi,k−Yi),\widehat{G}_{K_{n},\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Delta}}{{=}}\Sigma^{-1}\frac{1}{K_{n}}\sum_{k=1}^{K_{n}}\left\|X_{i,k}-Y_{i}\right\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{\beta-2}\left(X_{i,k}-Y_{i}\right),

with Xi,kX_{i,k} being samples from the correctly specified posterior P(⋅∣Y=Yi)P(\cdot\mid Y=Y_{i}), and KnK_{n} denoting the Monte Carlo budget such that the posterior-sampling error vanishes asymptotically. For this, we assume a similar empirical L2L_{2}-consistency in the evaluation sample as we did for the other score estimator:

1n​∑i=1nsupθ∈Θλ2​‖G^Kn,β,Σ​(Yi)−Gβ,Σ​(Yi)‖22=op​(1).\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\lambda^{2}\left\|\widehat{G}_{K_{n},\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})-G_{\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2}=o_{p}(1).

Thus, the argument follows along similar lines to the proof above. Defining

ai​(θ)=Δs^m,n​(Yi)−λ​Gβ,Σ​(Yi),Δi​(θ)=Δλ⁡(G^Kn,β,Σ​(Yi)−Gβ,Σ​(Yi)).a_{i}(\theta)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Delta}}{{=}}\widehat{s}_{m,n}(Y_{i})-\lambda G_{\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i}),\quad\Delta_{i}(\theta)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Delta}}{{=}}\lambda\left(\widehat{G}_{K_{n},\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})-G_{\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})\right).

Then the Monte Carlo residual satisfies

s^m,n​(Yi)−λ​G^Kn,β,Σ​(Yi)=ai​(θ)−Δi​(θ).\widehat{s}_{m,n}(Y_{i})-\lambda\widehat{G}_{K_{n},\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})=a_{i}(\theta)-\Delta_{i}(\theta).

Therefore, for each θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta,

J^n,KnMC​(θ)−J^n​(θ)\displaystyle\widehat{J}_{n,K_{n}}^{\mathrm{MC}}(\theta)-\widehat{J}_{n}(\theta) =1n​∑i=1n(‖ai​(θ)−Δi​(θ)‖22−‖ai​(θ)‖22)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\|a_{i}(\theta)-\Delta_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}-\|a_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}\right)
=1n​∑i=1n(−2​⟨ai​(θ),Δi​(θ)⟩+‖Δi​(θ)‖22).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(-2\langle a_{i}(\theta),\Delta_{i}(\theta)\rangle+\|\Delta_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}\right).

Taking the supremum and applying Cauchy–Schwarz as before gives

supθ∈Θ|J^n,KnMC​(θ)−J^n​(θ)|\displaystyle\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left|\widehat{J}_{n,K_{n}}^{\mathrm{MC}}(\theta)-\widehat{J}_{n}(\theta)\right| ≤2n​∑i=1nsupθ∈Θ‖ai​(θ)‖2​‖Δi​(θ)‖2+1n​∑i=1nsupθ∈Θ‖Δi​(θ)‖22\displaystyle\leq\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|a_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}\|\Delta_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|\Delta_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}
≤2​(1n​∑i=1nsupθ∈Θ‖ai​(θ)‖22)1/2​(1n​∑i=1nsupθ∈Θ‖Δi​(θ)‖22)1/2\displaystyle\leq 2\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|a_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}\right)^{1/2}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|\Delta_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}\right)^{1/2}
+1n∑i=1nsupθ∈Θ∥Δi(θ)∥22.\displaystyle+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|\Delta_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}.

The second part of the first term and the last term are op​(1)o_{p}(1) by assumption, since:

‖Δi​(θ)‖22=λ2​‖G^Kn,β,Σ​(Yi)−Gβ,Σ​(Yi)‖22.\|\Delta_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}=\lambda^{2}\left\|\widehat{G}_{K_{n},\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})-G_{\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2}.

Thus, the question is what is the order of 1n​∑i=1nsupθ∈Θ‖ai​(θ)‖22\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|a_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}? Reusing notation from the first part of the proof:

ei=s^m,n​(Yi)−sm​(Yi),ri​(θ)=sm​(Yi)−λ​Gβ,Σ​(Yi),e_{i}=\widehat{s}_{m,n}(Y_{i})-s_{m}(Y_{i}),\quad r_{i}(\theta)=s_{m}(Y_{i})-\lambda G_{\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i}),

we have:

ai​(θ)=s^m,n​(Yi)−λ​Gβ,Σ​(Yi)=ei+ri​(θ).a_{i}(\theta)=\widehat{s}_{m,n}(Y_{i})-\lambda G_{\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})=e_{i}+r_{i}(\theta).

Now, using the triangle inequality:

1n​∑i=1nsupθ∈Θ‖ai​(θ)‖22≤2n​∑i=1n‖ei‖22+2n​∑i=1nsupθ∈Θ‖ri​(θ)‖22.\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|a_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|e_{i}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|r_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}.

The first term is, as discussed, op​(1)o_{p}(1) by assumption; for the second term we have:

2n​∑i=1nsupθ∈Θ‖ri​(θ)‖22=2n​∑i=1nsupθ∈Θ‖sm​(Yi)−λ​Gβ,Σ​(Yi)‖22=Op​(1)\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|r_{i}(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left\|s_{m}(Y_{i})-\lambda G_{\beta,\Sigma}(Y_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2}=O_{p}(1)

by assumption on the oracle residual of the Energy-Tweedie term in the Proposition. Thus:

supθ∈Θ|J^n,KnMC​(θ)−J^n​(θ)|=op​(1).\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left|\widehat{J}_{n,K_{n}}^{\mathrm{MC}}(\theta)-\widehat{J}_{n}(\theta)\right|=o_{p}(1).

By the triangle inequality, we now have:

supθ∈Θ|J^n,KnMC​(θ)−J0​(θ)|≤supθ∈Θ|J^n,KnMC​(θ)−J^n​(θ)|+supθ∈Θ|J^n​(θ)−J0​(θ)|=op​(1).\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left|\widehat{J}_{n,K_{n}}^{\mathrm{MC}}(\theta)-J_{0}(\theta)\right|\leq\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left|\widehat{J}_{n,K_{n}}^{\mathrm{MC}}(\theta)-\widehat{J}_{n}(\theta)\right|+\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|\widehat{J}_{n}(\theta)-J_{0}(\theta)|=o_{p}(1).

Thus, for any θ^n,KnMC\widehat{\theta}^{\mathrm{MC}}_{n,K_{n}} satisfying:

J^n,KnMC​(θ^n,KnMC)≤infθ∈ΘJ^n,KnMC​(θ)+op​(1)\widehat{J}_{n,K_{n}}^{\mathrm{MC}}(\widehat{\theta}^{\mathrm{MC}}_{n,K_{n}})\leq\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\widehat{J}_{n,K_{n}}^{\mathrm{MC}}(\theta)+o_{p}(1)

the same argument as above applies, giving us:

θ^n,KnMC→Pθ∗.\widehat{\theta}^{\mathrm{MC}}_{n,K_{n}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle P}}{{\rightarrow}}\theta^{*}.

Proof of Corollary A.3

Starting from the population objective J0​(β,λ,Σ)J_{0}(\beta,\lambda,\Sigma), and fixing β\beta and Σ\Sigma, define

G(y;β,Σ)=ΔΣ−1𝔼X∼P(⋅∣Y=y)[∥X−y∥Σ−1β−2(X−y)].G(y;\beta,\Sigma)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Delta}}{{=}}\Sigma^{-1}~{\mathbb{E}}_{X\sim P(\cdot\mid Y=y)}\left[\|X-y\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{\beta-2}(X-y)\right].

Then:

J0\displaystyle J_{0} =𝔼Y∼m[∥sm(Y)+λβ∇YPDESΣ−1,β(P(⋅∣Y),Y)∥2]\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}\big[\|s_{m}(Y)+\frac{\lambda}{\beta}\nabla_{Y}^{\mathrm{PD}}\mathrm{ES}_{\Sigma^{-1},\beta}(P(\cdot\mid Y),Y)\|^{2}\big]
=𝔼Y∼m​[‖sm​(Y)−λ​G​(Y,β,Σ)‖2]\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}\big[\|s_{m}(Y)-\lambda G(Y;\beta,\Sigma)\|^{2}\big]
=𝔼Y∼m​[‖sm​(Y)‖22−2​λ​⟨sm​(Y),G⁡(Y,β,Σ)⟩+λ2​‖G⁡(Y,β,Σ)‖22].\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}\big[\|s_{m}(Y)\|_{2}^{2}-2\lambda\langle s_{m}(Y),G(Y;\beta,\Sigma)\rangle+\lambda^{2}\|G(Y;\beta,\Sigma)\|_{2}^{2}\big].

Setting the first-order condition ∂J0∂λ=0\frac{\partial J_{0}}{\partial\lambda}=0 gives, when 𝔼Y∼m​[‖G⁡(Y,β,Σ)‖22]>0{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}[\|G(Y;\beta,\Sigma)\|_{2}^{2}]>0:

λ∗​(β,Σ)=𝔼Y∼m​[⟨sm​(Y),G⁡(Y,β,Σ)⟩]𝔼Y∼m​[‖G⁡(Y,β,Σ)‖22].\lambda^{*}(\beta,\Sigma)=\frac{{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}\left[\langle s_{m}(Y),G(Y;\beta,\Sigma)\rangle\right]}{{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}\left[\|G(Y;\beta,\Sigma)\|^{2}_{2}\right]}.

Now, in the anisotropic Gaussian case β=2\beta=2, we have

G⁡(Y,2,Σ)=Σ−1​(𝔼⁡[X∣Y]−Y).G(Y;2,\Sigma)=\Sigma^{-1}\left({\mathbb{E}}[X\mid Y]-Y\right).

Hence:

λ∗​(β=2,Σ)=𝔼Y∼m​[⟨sm​(Y),Σ−1​(𝔼⁡[X∣Y]−Y)⟩]𝔼Y∼m​[‖Σ−1​(𝔼⁡[X∣Y]−Y)‖22].\lambda^{*}(\beta=2,\Sigma)=\frac{{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}\left[\left\langle s_{m}(Y),\Sigma^{-1}\left({\mathbb{E}}[X\mid Y]-Y\right)\right\rangle\right]}{{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}\left[\left\|\Sigma^{-1}\left({\mathbb{E}}[X\mid Y]-Y\right)\right\|^{2}_{2}\right]}.

λ∗​(β=2,σ2​Id)=σ2​𝔼Y∼m​[⟨sm​(Y),𝔼⁡[X∣Y]−Y⟩]𝔼Y∼m​[‖𝔼⁡[X∣Y]−Y‖22].\lambda^{*}(\beta=2,\sigma^{2}I_{d})=\sigma^{2}\frac{{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}\left[\left\langle s_{m}(Y),{\mathbb{E}}[X\mid Y]-Y\right\rangle\right]}{{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim m}\left[\left\|{\mathbb{E}}[X\mid Y]-Y\right\|^{2}_{2}\right]}.

A.6.1 Diffusion Along Arbitrary Noise-Parameter Paths: Eight Gaussians

This section details the five-parameter Eight-Gaussians experiment summarized in Sec. 5.3. The noise law is the generalized Gaussian of Eq. 16 with the trace-normalized shape matrix S⁡(u,v)=(1+uvv1−u)S(u,v)=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1+u&v\\ v&1-u\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) parameterized by disk coordinates u2+v2<1u^{2}+v^{2}<1. The schedules below prescribe rtr_{t}, which fixes the reference RMS ρt=rt​λt1/βt\rho_{t}=r_{t}\,\lambda_{t}^{1/\beta_{t}} along any path. The full conditioning vector is (β,log⁡λ,log⁡ρ,u,v)(\beta,\log\lambda,\log\rho,u,v). The four reverse sampling paths of Sec. 5.3, stated over path progress t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], are:

Isotropic, fixed tail:\displaystyle\text{Isotropic, fixed tail:} (βt,λt,ut,vt)=(1.4, 1.8, 0, 0),\displaystyle(\beta_{t},\lambda_{t},u_{t},v_{t})=(1.4,\,1.8,\,0,\,0), (52)
Fixed non-diagonal, fixed tail:\displaystyle\text{Fixed non-diagonal, fixed tail:} (βt,λt,ut,vt)=(1.4, 1.8, 0, 0.6),\displaystyle(\beta_{t},\lambda_{t},u_{t},v_{t})=(1.4,\,1.8,\,0,\,0.6),
Rotating covariance, fixed tail:\displaystyle\text{Rotating covariance, fixed tail:} (βt,λt)=(1.4, 1.8),(ut,vt)=0.6(cosθt,sinθt),\displaystyle(\beta_{t},\lambda_{t})=(1.4,\,1.8),\quad(u_{t},v_{t})=0.6\,(\cos\theta_{t},\sin\theta_{t}),
θt=π2+2​π​t,\displaystyle\theta_{t}=\tfrac{\pi}{2}+2\pi t,
Joint five-parameter path:\displaystyle\text{Joint five-parameter path:} βt=1.4+0.5sin2(πt),λt=1.8+0.4sin(2πt),\displaystyle\beta_{t}=1.4+0.5\sin^{2}(\pi t),\quad\lambda_{t}=1.8+0.4\sin(2\pi t),
(ut,vt)​as rotating.\displaystyle(u_{t},v_{t})\ \text{as rotating}.

Figure 8 displays the four noise-parameter paths. The parameter-path panel plots rtr_{t}, ρt\rho_{t}, and (βt,λt,ut,vt)(\beta_{t},\lambda_{t},u_{t},v_{t}) against path progress tt; all four paths share the schedule rtr_{t}.

Figure 9 shows the full one-parameter score-field sweeps behind Fig. 1: each row varies one conditioning parameter while the remaining parameters stay at the base parameter combination (β,λ,ρ,u,v)=(1.4, 1.8, 0.57, 0, 0.6)(\beta,\lambda,\rho,u,v)=(1.4,\,1.8,\,0.57,\,0,\,0.6) (the uu and vv rows set the respective other disk coordinate to zero). From top to bottom, the rows use β∈{1.3,1.5,1.75,2.0}\beta\in\{1.3,1.5,1.75,2.0\}, λ∈{1.0,1.4,1.8,2.5}\lambda\in\{1.0,1.4,1.8,2.5\}, ρ∈{0.13,0.32,0.57,0.95}\rho\in\{0.13,0.32,0.57,0.95\} (the σ\sigma sweep of App. A.4.2), u∈{−0.6,…,0.6}u\in\{-0.6,\dots,0.6\}, and v∈{−0.6,…,0.6}v\in\{-0.6,\dots,0.6\}. Streamlines show normalized score direction and color shows magnitude. The field responds to each parameter as expected: raising β\beta toward 22 moves the field from center-seeking toward the mean-seeking, ring-concentrating Gaussian regime, λ\lambda and ρ\rho rescale the field and the noise magnitude, and (u,v)(u,v) tilt the field along the corresponding covariance geometry.

Generation protocol.

We train two independent five-parameter conditional Engression models (training seeds 42 and 43) and sample each along the four reverse paths of Eq. 52, sharing one RMS schedule: 5151 geometrically spaced levels with rtr_{t} decreasing from 0.830.83 to 0.00830.0083. The rotating covariance completes a full rotation over the path, and the joint path matches rtr_{t} at every level through ρt\rho_{t}, with endpoints pinned to the rotating path — the joint-vs-rotating comparison therefore isolates the intermediate route through (β,λ,ρ)(\beta,\lambda,\rho). Sampling uses annealed Langevin with 1010 steps per level and N=64N=64 posterior draws per score evaluation; each model is sampled with three seeds of 4,0964{,}096 final samples, pooled to 12,28812{,}288 samples per model and path. Signed energy distance to clean data is computed on fixed seed-stratified 4,0964{,}096-sample subsets against an independent 4,0964{,}096-point clean reference; mode coverage and radial error use all pooled samples.

Table 11 reports mean ±\pm sample standard deviation across the two trained models. Its endpoint metrics are signed energy distance to clean data, total variation from uniform mode weights, minimum mode mass, and mean radial distance to the ring; the final row is an independent clean-sample reference of the same size.

All eight modes retain more than 1%1\% mass on every path, run, and model. The four paths have similar endpoint estimates, and the paired joint-minus-rotating differences are negligible: signed ED 0.00002±0.000300.00002\pm 0.00030, mode-weight TV −0.0031±0.0014-0.0031\pm 0.0014, minimum mode mass 0.0007±0.00010.0007\pm 0.0001, mean radial error −0.0073±0.0020-0.0073\pm 0.0020. Routing the reverse process through simultaneously varying (β,λ,σ)(\beta,\lambda,\sigma) therefore incurs no measurable endpoint cost relative to the matched covariance-only control.

Figures 11 and 12 show the endpoint samples and the reverse-chain states along the schedule.

Figure 10 tracks the reverse chain against the exact noisy marginal at each level: the distance drops from 0.0150.015–0.0280.028 at rt=0.53r_{t}=0.53 to 0.0030.003–0.0060.006 at rt=0.33r_{t}=0.33 and remains near zero thereafter on all four paths, indicating that the sampler follows the intended sequence of noisy marginals rather than only reaching a good endpoint. This check also covers the small-noise levels, where importance sampling no longer provides a reliable ground-truth score.

Fixed-parameter path isolation.

We additionally compare constant-parameter paths: along each path, (β,λ,u,v)(\beta,\lambda,u,v) stay fixed and only the RMS rtr_{t} decreases. Each arm changes a single coordinate of the reference value (β,λ,u,v)=(1.4,1.8,0,0.6)(\beta,\lambda,u,v)=(1.4,1.8,0,0.6) and holds it for the entire path, so differences against the reference arm isolate the contribution of that coordinate. All arms use the same two trained five-parameter posterior models, three sampling seeds per model, a shared 4949-level RMS schedule rtr_{t} from 0.83290.8329 to 0.01000.0100, and identical Langevin and posterior-sampling budgets. Each run produces 4,0964{,}096 endpoint draws; the three runs are pooled within each model before nonlinear metrics are computed. Table 12 reports mean ±\pm sample standard deviation across the two trained models. The tracking maximum is the largest signed energy distance to the exact noisy marginal over the post-burn-in checkpoints and is distinct from endpoint quality. Signed energy distance uses a fixed seed-stratified subset of 4,0964{,}096 generated draws and an independent clean reference of the same size; mode metrics use all 12,28812{,}288 pooled draws per trained model.

Covariance geometry gives the clearest endpoint differences. Relative to the reference fixed path, (u,v)=(0.6,0)(u,v)=(0.6,0) lowers signed ED from 0.007460.00746 to 0.003570.00357 and mode-weight TV from 0.04610.0461 to 0.02200.0220, while raising minimum mode mass from 0.10560.1056 to 0.11510.1151. The radial parameters have smaller or metric-dependent effects: β=1.8\beta=1.8 improves all four reported metrics, while λ=1\lambda=1 gives the lowest tracking point estimate but nearly unchanged endpoint signed ED. Endpoint quality and worst-case marginal tracking therefore induce different descriptive rankings; with two trained-model seeds, the table is to be read more as a preliminary exploration.

A.6.2 Energy-Tweedie Diffusion on MNIST

This section details the MNIST experiment summarized in Sec. 5.3. The posterior model is a single conditional Engression network (hidden width 2,5602{,}560) conditioned on the five-parameter noise specification (β,λ,ρ,u,v)(\beta,\lambda,\rho,u,v), with the reference RMS ρ\rho of Eq. 42 and d=784d=784. Training uses ρ∈[0.025,6]\rho\in[0.025,6], β∈[1.3,2]\beta\in[1.3,2], λ∈[1,2.5]\lambda\in[1,2.5], and covariance-disk radius ‖(u,v)‖≤0.7\|(u,v)\|\leq 0.7. Generalized / isotropic:\displaystyle\text{Generalized / isotropic:} (βt,λt,ut,vt)=(1.4, 1.8, 0, 0),\displaystyle(\beta_{t},\lambda_{t},u_{t},v_{t})=(1.4,\,1.8,\,0,\,0),
Generalized / non-diagonal:\displaystyle\text{Generalized / non-diagonal:} (βt,λt,ut,vt)=(1.4, 1.8, 0, 0.6),\displaystyle(\beta_{t},\lambda_{t},u_{t},v_{t})=(1.4,\,1.8,\,0,\,0.6),
Joint five-parameter path:\displaystyle\text{Joint five-parameter path:} βt=2−0.6t,λt=1+0.8t,ut=0.3sin(πt),vt=0.6t.\displaystyle\beta_{t}=2-0.6t,\quad\lambda_{t}=1+0.8t,\quad u_{t}=0.3\sin(\pi t),\quad v_{t}=0.6t.

Figure 13 displays the five sampling paths. The path panel plots (ρt,rt,βt,λt,ut,vt)(\rho_{t},r_{t},\beta_{t},\lambda_{t},u_{t},v_{t}) against path progress and includes the (u,v)(u,v) trajectories inside the training region.

The Gaussian/isotropic path is ordinary Gaussian diffusion, where Eq. 32 reduces to the posterior-mean Tweedie residual. The joint path starts at the Gaussian/isotropic start and ends at the generalized/non-diagonal endpoint, so the corruption transitions continuously from isotropic Gaussian into a heavy-tailed anisotropic law as the noise shrinks, and was not tuned for performance.

Sampling uses annealed Langevin with 1,0001{,}000 updates at the first level and 100100 at each subsequent level, N=256N=256 posterior draws per score evaluation, a shared step-size curve, and a final posterior draw at the terminal level rt=0.197r_{t}=0.197. Each path is sampled with three seeds (27182718, 31413141, 57725772) of 256256 images, pooled to 768768 images per path; every generated image enters the evaluation without any selection.

Evaluation.

The primary metric is the signed unbiased energy distance between penultimate-layer features of a fixed, publicly available MNIST classifier (ONNX Model Zoo MNIST-12; 256256-dimensional features; test accuracy 0.9890.989), computed between generated samples and a fixed bank of 2,0482{,}048 held-out real images. The classifier features discard pixel-level nuisance variation while any discrepancy in feature space shows a discrepancy between the underlying distributions; the energy distance admits an unbiased estimator and equals twice the squared maximum mean discrepancy for the associated distance-induced kernel [42; 32], making it a close relative of the kernel inception distance [3] while remaining within the energy-score toolkit used throughout this paper. Because the estimator is unbiased, its scale has a direct null reference: repeated real-vs-real draws of disjoint held-out images with the identical estimator and reference bank give a null distribution whose 9595th percentile at the pooled sample size is 0.0170.017. Companion metrics are the mean classifier confidence and the total variation between the predicted class distribution and the test-set class prior. Reported values are pooled point estimates over 768768 images per path with seed-stratified 95%95\% bootstrap confidence intervals. The real-vs-real feature energy distance is reported without a percentile interval because the energy distance is a degenerate U-statistic at the null; the measured null distribution supplies its reference scale instead.

All ten classes are present on every path. The two fixed non-diagonal paths give the lowest feature energy distances. The generalized/non-diagonal path has the best point estimate on all three metrics, although its intervals overlap those of the Gaussian/non-diagonal path. Both isotropic paths have larger feature energy distance, while the joint path lies between the non-diagonal and isotropic controls. As a memorization check, mean pixel RMSE to the nearest training image is 0.1390.139–0.1430.143 across the generated paths, compared with 0.1470.147 for held-out real images. Figure 14 pairs generated examples with their nearest training neighbors, showing similar strokes and poses without exact pixel-space duplicates. It contains twelve unselected endpoint samples from the common figure seed for each path.

Figures 15 and 16 show the reverse chains at matched rtr_{t} and the endpoint samples for each path and seed. The progress grid uses paths as columns and matched-RMS levels as rows, with the same nine chains in each cell.

A.7 Further Connections

We present some further connective threads to the work presented in this section, specializing again to the generalized Gaussian case.

A.7.1 Connection Between the Noise Geometry and the Energy Score Loss

As indicated by Theorem 20, there is a correspondence between each noising distribution parameterized by β,λ,Σ\beta,\lambda,\Sigma and an energy score with the same parameters whose path-derivative matches the score of the data noised by the former.

One perspective is to notice that the Mahalanobis distance ∥⋅∥Σ−1\|\cdot\|_{\Sigma^{-1}} can be associated to the (position-independent) Riemannian inner product ⟨u,v⟩=uT​Σ−1​v\langle u,v\rangle=u^{T}\Sigma^{-1}v. We thus get for the Riemannian gradient gradΣ−1⁡f⁡(x)=Σ​∇xf​(x).\operatorname{grad}_{\Sigma^{-1}}f(x)=\Sigma~\nabla_{x}f(x). Now, one can define the Riemannian path-derivative analogously to the ordinary one, and get that, by Eq. 17 the noisy score is proportional to the Riemannian gradient of some potential/energy:

sm​(y)=−λ​Σ−1​𝔼​[‖y−X‖Σ−1β−2​(y−X)∣Y=y]=−λ​Σ−1​gradΣ−1PD⁡φ⁡(y),s_{m}(y)=-\lambda~\Sigma^{-1}\,{\mathbb{E}}\left[\|y-X\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{\beta-2}~(y-X)\mid Y=y\right]=-\lambda~\Sigma^{-1}\operatorname{grad}^{\mathrm{PD}}_{\Sigma^{-1}}\varphi(y),

where we can solve for φ⁡(y)\varphi(y) and obtain:

φ⁡(y)=1β​𝔼​[‖y−X‖Σ−1β∣Y=y],\varphi(y)=\frac{1}{\beta}~{\mathbb{E}}[\|y-X\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{\beta}\mid Y=y],

i.e., the “mean β\beta-energy” associated with the posterior (w.r.t. YY) of the generalized Gaussian elliptical distribution (i.e., “energy model”) — cf. Eq. 16 — in the geometry induced by Σ\Sigma.

A.7.2 Denoising

Denoising can be seen as both a problem setting and a generative modeling approach [23]. In this subsection, we first focus on the denoising problem as such, with the generative modeling presented in Sec. 5.3.

In this case, the posterior P⁡(X∣Y=y)P(X\mid Y=y) can be considered a distributional denoiser with Pθ​(X∣Y=y)P_{\theta}(X\mid Y=y) denoting its estimator. An example of score-based denoising is Kim and Ye [17], who have focused on using the standard Tweedie formula in the denoising context, using denoising autoencoders [46] to extract the score. The vast majority of denoising work limits the noise to the isotropic Gaussian 𝒩⁡(0,σ2​I){\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^{2}I).

An interesting perspective is to consider ideal denoisers in light of our results. As noted in Milanfar and Delbracio [23], if f⁡(y,α)f(y,\alpha) denotes the denoising functional for noise level parameters α\alpha44 4 One can consider α\alpha to be a vector in this case., then the ideal denoiser will be a gradient of some scalar function (the “energy” or potential):

f⋆​(y,α)=∇𝒰​(y,α),f^{\star}(y,\alpha)=\nabla{\mathcal{U}}(y,\alpha),

which is equivalent to requiring that its Jacobian be symmetric in the isotropic Gaussian case. Thus, the denoiser itself defines a conservative vector field. We will be focusing on MSE-optimal denoisers in the following discussion.

In the isotropic Gaussian case, this is readily apparent from the “basic” Tweedie formula:

f⋆​(y,σ2)=𝔼⁡[X∣Y=y]=y+σ2​∇y​log⁡m⁡(y)f^{\star}(y,\sigma^{2})\;=\;{\mathbb{E}}[X\!\mid Y{=}y]\;=\;y+\sigma^{2}\,\nabla_{y}\log m(y)

implies for the Jacobian:

∇f⋆​(y,σ2)=I+σ2​∇2​log⁡m⁡(y),\nabla f^{\star}(y,\sigma^{2})=I+\sigma^{2}\nabla^{2}\!\log m(y),

which is obviously symmetric.

Moving to the anisotropic Gaussian case — α=(β=2,λ=1,Σ)\alpha=(\beta=2,\lambda=1,\Sigma) — we still have Eq. 5:

f⋆​(y,α)=y+Σ​∇y​log⁡m⁡(y).f^{\star}(y,\alpha)\;=\;y+\Sigma\,\nabla_{y}\log m(y).

By App. A.7.1, this can be seen as the Riemannian gradient in the geometry induced by Σ\Sigma:

f⋆​(y,α)=gradΣ−1⁡(12​‖y‖Σ−12+log⁡m⁡(y))⏟𝒰,f^{\star}(y,\alpha)\;=\;\operatorname{grad}_{\Sigma^{-1}}\!\underbrace{\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}\|y\|^{2}_{\Sigma^{-1}}+\log m(y)\Big)}_{{\mathcal{U}}}, (54)

where 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} is the potential function mentioned above for this case. The Jacobian of such an ideal denoiser:

∇f⋆​(y)=I+Σ​∇2​log⁡m⁡(y)\nabla f^{\star}(y)=I+\Sigma\nabla^{2}\!\log m(y)

is not necessarily symmetric (as it depends on Σ\Sigma, i.e. the anisotropy). However, we have:

(∇f⋆(y))⊤Σ−1=Σ−1∇f⋆(y),(\nabla f^{\star}(y))^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}=\Sigma^{-1}\nabla f^{\star}(y), (55)

i.e., it is self-adjoint in the Σ−1\Sigma^{-1} geometry, or equivalently, it is symmetric in whitened coordinates. This represents a generalization of the criterion for ideal denoisers to anisotropic Gaussian noise — self-adjointness.

A common alternative MAP-optimal denoiser fMAP​(y,α)f_{\mathrm{MAP}}(y,\alpha) can be obtained from the proximal operator [23; 4]:

proxRΣ−1⁡(y)=arg​minx⁡(12​‖x−y‖Σ−12+R⁡(x)),\operatorname{prox}_{R}^{\Sigma^{-1}}(y)=\argmin_{x}(\tfrac{1}{2}\|x-y\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}+R(x)),

where R⁡(x)R(x) is the negative log-prior on the clean data xx. Under additive Gaussian noise, the MAP estimator is the proximal operator of the negative log-prior. If the prior is also Gaussian, then the posterior is Gaussian, so the MAP estimate coincides with the posterior mean (equivalently, the Wiener filter); hence the resulting field matches Eq. 54.

Finally, still in the anisotropic Gaussian case, we have by Tweedie:

f⋆​(y)−y=Σ​sm​(y).f^{\star}(y)-y=\Sigma\,s_{m}(y)\;.

However, by Thm. 20, we also have:

f⋆​(y)−y=−Σ2​∇yPDESΣ−1,2​(P⁡(X∣Y=y),y).f^{\star}(y)-y=-\frac{\Sigma}{2}\nabla_{y}^{\mathrm{PD}}\mathrm{ES}_{\Sigma^{-1},2}\big(P(X\mid Y=y),y\big). (56)

Thus, the potential 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} that generates the conservative field is defined either by the log-marginal log⁡m⁡(y)\log m(y) (as previously shown in Eq. 54) or the corresponding energy score as denoted by Eq. 56:

gradΣ−1⁡(12​‖y‖Σ−12+log⁡m⁡(y))\displaystyle\operatorname{grad}_{\Sigma^{-1}}\!\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}\|y\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}\,+\,\log m(y)\Big) =f⋆​(y)\displaystyle=\;f^{\star}(y) (57)
=gradΣ−1PD⁡(12​‖y‖Σ−12−12​ESΣ−1,2​(P⁡(X∣Y=y),y)),\displaystyle=\;\operatorname{grad}^{\mathrm{PD}}_{\Sigma^{-1}}\!\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}\|y\|_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}\;-\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{ES}_{\Sigma^{-1},2}\!\big(P(X\mid Y=y),y\big)\Big),

with the caveat that in the latter case, we need to take the path derivative ∇yPD\nabla_{y}^{\mathrm{PD}} (Eq. 14).

A.8 Model Architectures and Training

Our posterior models adapt the implementation of Shen and Meinshausen [35]55 5 https://github.com/xwshen51/engression: stochastic residual MLPs conditioned on the noise parameters, with architectures summarized in Table 14. We train these models on clean–noisy pairs using the Euclidean energy score with exponent one for the non-diffusion use cases. Noise parameters enter through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM): the noise scale for isotropic models, scale and covariance shape for parameter estimation, and all five noise parameters for the five-parameter Eight-Gaussians and MNIST models.

All posteriors use Adam with cosine learning-rate decay. Eight-Gaussians training accumulates two minibatches per optimizer step; MNIST uses one, with a 500500-step learning-rate warmup. Each fixed or five-parameter Eight-Gaussians posterior is reused for score estimation and diffusion; all five MNIST sampling paths share one posterior model.

The five-parameter Eight-Gaussians posterior draws one noise-parameter combination per minibatch: with probability 0.350.35 one of 1818 preselected combinations, namely (β,λ)=(1.4,1.8)(\beta,\lambda)=(1.4,1.8) at the reference RMS levels ρ∈{0.32,0.57,0.95}\rho\in\{0.32,0.57,0.95\} (Eq. 42) and the covariance shapes (u,v)∈{(0,0),(0.6,0),(0,0.6),(0.6/2,0.6/2)}(u,v)\in\{(0,0),(0.6,0),(0,0.6),(0.6/\sqrt{2},0.6/\sqrt{2})\} together with six extremal parameter combinations, and otherwise β\beta uniform on [1.3,2][1.3,2], λ\lambda and ρ\rho log-uniform on [1,2.5][1,2.5] and [0.01,10][0.01,10], and (u,v)(u,v) uniform in area on the disk of radius 0.70.7.

For plug-in parameter estimation, we reuse one score estimation network across the three noise-level settings in each replicate. Conditioning on the known log noise level avoids training three separate Hyvärinen networks; the method itself is parameter-agnostic (i.e., this is to save on compute, not required by the method). Each network has three hidden layers of width 256256 with SiLU activations and is trained by exact Hyvärinen score matching, using AdamW for 40,00040{,}000 steps with batch size 4,0964{,}096 and learning rate 10−310^{-3}. Complete training configurations, seeds, and preprocessing are provided in the supplement.

For the direct-score comparison in Sec. 5.1, ET-DSM and Hyvärinen use the MLP architecture described above, with seven inputs: the two noisy coordinates and the normalized conditioning vector (β,log⁡λ,log⁡ρ,u,v)(\beta,\log\lambda,\log\rho,u,v), with the reference RMS ρ\rho defined in Eq. 42. The linear output layer outputs the two score coordinates.

We train each network for 80,00080{,}000 AdamW updates with batch size 4,0964{,}096, cosine learning-rate decay from 10−310^{-3} to 10−510^{-5}, zero weight decay, and gradient clipping at norm 1010. Each minibatch uses one noise-parameter combination; the two estimators receive the same minibatches in order.
